items.title: Introduction to dbt (data build tool)
items.body:
## Introduction to dbt (data build tool)

dbt is the tool that turned analytics SQL into real software engineering, and it is increasingly on BI/analytics-engineer job postings. The idea: instead of a pile of ad-hoc SQL scripts and hand-built views, you define your transformations as version-controlled **models** (SELECT statements) that dbt runs, tests, and documents.

What dbt actually gives you:
- **Models as SQL files in git.** Each model is a `SELECT` that becomes a view or table in the warehouse. Your `region_summary` view from last week becomes a tracked, reviewable model.
- **`ref()` and dependency management.** Models reference each other with `{{ ref('stg_orders') }}`; dbt works out the build order automatically and builds the whole DAG. This is how you layer raw -> staging -> marts cleanly.
- **Tests.** Declare expectations (`unique`, `not_null`, accepted values, relationships) and dbt checks them on every run, so a broken upstream change is caught before it reaches a dashboard.
- **Documentation + lineage.** dbt generates docs and a visual lineage graph showing how every table flows from source to report.

The mental model: dbt is the **transformation (T) layer** of modern ELT, raw data lands in the warehouse, dbt transforms it into clean, tested, documented reporting models, and BI tools read those. It brings software practices (version control, testing, modularity, review) to the SQL that BI depends on.

You do not need to master dbt this week, you need to understand what it is and why it exists, because "have you used dbt?" is now a common screen. items.title: Modern data stack overview
items.body:
## The modern data stack

"Modern data stack" is the phrase for the now-standard set of cloud tools BI runs on. Knowing the pieces, and which job each does, lets you speak the language in any data interview.

The standard flow is **ELT** (Extract, Load, Transform, the modern reordering of old ETL):
1. **Extract + Load (ingestion):** tools like Fivetran, Airbyte, or Stitch copy raw data from sources (apps, databases, SaaS APIs) *into* the warehouse, with little transformation. Load first, transform later.
2. **Store (the cloud warehouse):** BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift, or Databricks. Cheap storage, massive parallel query power. This is the centre of gravity.
3. **Transform:** dbt (yesterday) turns the raw loaded data into clean, modelled, tested reporting tables, *inside* the warehouse.
4. **Serve (BI):** Power BI, Looker, Tableau, Metabase read the transformed models and present them.
5. **Orchestrate + observe:** Airflow/Dagster schedule the pipeline; tools like Monte Carlo watch for data quality issues.

Why ELT replaced ETL: cloud warehouses are so powerful and cheap that it is easier to load raw data and transform it *in* the warehouse (with SQL/dbt) than to transform it in transit. That one architectural shift is why dbt and warehouses like Snowflake exploded.

Where you fit: a BI analyst lives mostly in **Transform (dbt/SQL)** and **Serve (Power BI)**, and needs literacy in the rest. Today, draw the stack for an imaginary company (source -> Fivetran -> Snowflake -> dbt -> Power BI) and label what each layer does. That diagram is a great whiteboard answer to "walk me through a modern data pipeline."

items.body: OLTP and OLAP are two database worlds optimised for opposite jobs, and confusing them is why some reports crawl. OLTP (Online Transaction Processing) powers the live application, many tiny, fast reads and writes, like 'insert this order' or 'update this customer', and is structured (highly normalised) to make those single-row operations safe and quick. OLAP (Online Analytical Processing) powers analytics, a few enormous queries that scan and aggregate millions of rows, like 'total sales by region by month for three years', and is structured (star schemas, columnar storage) to make those sweeping aggregations fast. A query like that three-year roll-up flies on OLAP but crawls on OLTP, because OLTP was never built to scan everything. Give me one specific query that is fast on OLAP and slow on OLTP, and explain what about each design causes the difference.

weeks.title: Business Statistics for BI
weeks.context:
BI without statistics is opinion dressed as data. Business statistics gives you the tools to separate signal from noise, quantify uncertainty, and make claims about data that can be defended when challenged.

The statistics that BI analysts actually use daily: descriptive statistics (mean, median, standard deviation, percentiles), distributions (understanding what normal looks like so you can spot anomalies), correlation (does variable A move with variable B?), and regression (can I predict Y from X?).

The most important skill this week is statistical intuition, knowing when a trend is real versus random noise, when a correlation is meaningful versus coincidental, and when your sample size is too small to make a claim. These are the moments that determine whether a BI analyst is credible or not.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## Statistics: turning "I think" into "the data shows"

BI without statistics is opinion dressed up as charts. Statistics is what lets you say "sales are up" and *defend* it when a skeptical VP pushes back, separate a real trend from random noise, and put honest bounds on uncertainty. You do not need a maths degree; you need the handful of tools BI analysts use daily and the judgement to apply them.

This week covers exactly that practical core: describing data (averages that do not mislead), understanding distributions (so you pick the right average), correlation vs causation (the trap behind most bad data claims), spotting outliers, and the basics of probability. Next week builds on it with A/B testing.

The mindset shift: every number on a dashboard is a *sample* of a noisy reality, and your job is to know how much to trust it. "Conversion went from 4.0% to 4.3%", real improvement, or random wiggle? Statistics is the difference between confidently answering and guessing.

Today, orient with your Superstore data (in Power BI, SQL, or even Excel): compute a few summary numbers, average sales per order, the spread, and ask the questions you will learn to answer this week, "is the mean misleading here? are there outliers dragging it? is this month genuinely different or just noise?" Write those questions down; the week answers them.

items.title: Descriptive statistics
items.body:
## Descriptive statistics (and how averages lie)

Descriptive statistics summarise a dataset in a few numbers. The trap is using the wrong summary and getting misled.

**Centre, three flavours:**
- **Mean** (the average): sensitive to extremes. One whale order of 50,000 drags the mean sales-per-order way up, so it no longer describes a typical order.
- **Median** (the middle value): robust to extremes. For skewed business data (income, order value, time-on-site, almost always right-skewed), the **median is usually the honest "typical" number.**
- **Mode** (most common value): useful for categories.

The single most common analytics mistake: reporting the mean of skewed data. "Average order value is $340" when 90% of orders are under $100 and a few huge ones pull the mean up is technically true and practically a lie. Report the median, or both.

**Spread:**
- **Range** (max minus min): crude, dominated by outliers.
- **Standard deviation:** average distance from the mean, the standard "how spread out" measure. A small SD means values cluster near the mean; a large SD means high variability. Spread matters as much as centre: two regions with the same average sales but very different SDs are completely different businesses.
- **Percentiles / IQR:** the 25th–75th percentile range (IQR) describes the middle half, robust and intuitive ("half our orders fall between $40 and $180").

Today, on Superstore: compute mean *and* median sales per order and see how far apart they are (the gap reveals skew), plus the standard deviation and the IQR. Then write the one-sentence honest summary of "a typical order" using the median, not the mean. Knowing *which* statistic to report is the skill.

items.title: Distributions
items.body:
## Distributions: the shape behind the numbers

A distribution is the *shape* of how values spread, and the shape tells you which statistics and methods are valid. Looking at the distribution (a histogram) before computing anything is a habit that prevents most statistical mistakes.

The shapes you will meet:
- **Normal (bell curve):** symmetric around the mean, most values near the centre. Heights, measurement errors, and *averages of many things* tend toward normal. Many statistical tests assume it. But, crucially, most raw business metrics are NOT normal.
- **Right-skewed (long tail to the right):** the common one in business. Order values, customer lifetime value, page views, session length, a mass of small values and a long tail of big ones. Here the mean exceeds the median, and the median is the honest centre.
- **Bimodal (two peaks):** a sign you have two populations mixed together (e.g. weekday vs weekend traffic). The fix is usually to split them and analyse separately, an "average" across two peaks describes neither.
- **Uniform:** roughly flat; every value about equally likely.

Why it matters for BI: the distribution decides your choice of average (skewed -> median), whether a test is valid (many tests assume normality), and whether a single summary number even makes sense (bimodal -> it does not). The **central limit theorem** is the saving grace: even when raw data is skewed, the *averages of samples* trend normal, which is why averaging and many tests still work, a fact worth knowing for next week.

Today, plot a histogram of Superstore sales (Power BI, Python, or Excel). You will almost certainly see right-skew. Identify the shape, and state what it implies: median over mean, and watch for the long tail of high-value orders.

items.title: Correlation and causation
items.body:
## Correlation and causation (the trap behind bad claims)

"Correlation is not causation" is a cliché because analysts violate it constantly, and it is the single most dangerous mistake in BI, because it leads to confident, wrong decisions.

**Correlation** measures how two variables move together, quantified by the correlation coefficient **r**, from -1 (perfect inverse) through 0 (no linear relationship) to +1 (perfect positive). "Discount depth and units sold have r = 0.6" means they tend to rise together. Useful, and easy to compute.

**Causation** means one variable *makes* the other change. Correlation alone never proves it, for three reasons you must be able to name:
- **Confounding (lurking variable):** ice-cream sales and drownings correlate, because *summer* drives both. The hidden third variable creates the link.
- **Reverse causation:** maybe Y causes X, not X causes Y.
- **Coincidence:** with enough variables, some correlate by pure chance (spurious correlations).

For BI this is constant: "stores with our new layout have higher sales", is it the layout, or were those the flagship stores in rich areas (confounder)? "Customers who use the app spend more", does the app cause spend, or do high-spenders just adopt apps (reverse)?

The professional habits: (1) when you report a correlation, say "associated with", not "causes", unless you have an experiment; (2) actively ask "what could be confounding this?"; (3) remember the only clean way to establish causation is a **controlled experiment**, which is exactly next week's A/B testing.

Today, compute a correlation in Superstore (e.g. discount vs profit, you may find a *negative* one, deep discounts erode profit). Report it honestly as an association, and write one plausible confounder before you would ever claim cause.

items.title: Outlier detection
items.body:
## Outlier detection

Outliers, values far from the rest, are everywhere in business data, and how you handle them changes your conclusions. The discipline is to *find* them, *understand* them, then *decide*, never silently delete.

**Two standard detection methods:**
- **IQR method (robust, distribution-agnostic):** compute Q1, Q3, and IQR = Q3 − Q1. Flag values below Q1 − 1.5×IQR or above Q3 + 1.5×IQR. This is what a box plot's "whiskers" use; it works regardless of distribution, so it is the safe default for skewed business data.
- **Z-score method (for roughly normal data):** how many standard deviations a value is from the mean. |z| > 3 is a common flag. Only trustworthy when data is approximately normal, on skewed data it mis-flags.

The harder part is **judgement, not detection.** When you find an outlier, ask:
- **Is it an error?** A $1,000,000 order that is really a data-entry typo. Fix or remove, with a note.
- **Is it real and meaningful?** A genuine whale customer, or fraud, or a viral spike. This is often the *most important* data point, removing it hides the signal. Fraud detection is literally outlier hunting.
- **Is it distorting a summary?** A real but extreme value can wreck a mean (use median) or a model (consider analysing with and without it, and report both).

The rule: **investigate before you exclude, and document every exclusion.** Quietly dropping inconvenient points to make a chart look nice is how analysts lose trust, and sometimes how they hide the very thing that mattered.

Today, on Superstore: use the IQR method to flag outlier orders by sales, look at a few, and classify them (error? real whale?). Decide and document how you would treat them, and note how the mean changes if you exclude them.

items.title: Intro to probability
items.body:
## Intro to probability (enough to reason about uncertainty)

Probability is the language of uncertainty, and BI is full of it: "how likely is this month's dip to be just noise?", "what's the chance a customer churns?". You need the working basics, not measure theory.

The essentials:
- **Probability** is a number from 0 to 1 (or 0–100%) for how likely an event is. The probabilities of all possible outcomes sum to 1.
- **Independent vs dependent events.** Independent: one does not affect the other (two separate customers buying). Dependent: one changes the other's odds (a customer's second purchase given a first). For independent events, probabilities multiply: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
- **Conditional probability**, P(A given B), the chance of A *given that* B happened, is the heart of analytics. "Probability a visitor converts *given* they came from email" is conditional, and it is what most BI questions actually ask.
- **Expected value** = sum of (outcome × its probability). It is how you reason about decisions under uncertainty: the expected revenue of a campaign is each outcome's value weighted by its likelihood. Managers make bets; expected value is how you evaluate them.

Why a BI analyst cares: probability underpins everything in next week's hypothesis testing. A **p-value** (the core of A/B testing) is literally a conditional probability, "the probability of seeing data this extreme *if* there were truly no effect." Confidence intervals are probability statements about uncertainty. Get comfortable now and next week is far easier.

items.body: Mean and median both try to capture 'the typical value', but they react very differently to extremes, and knowing which to trust is what separates an analyst from a calculator. The mean adds everything up and divides by the count, so every value pulls on it, including one giant outlier. The median is the middle value when you line the data up in order, so it ignores how extreme the extremes are. weeks.title: A/B Testing and Hypothesis Testing
weeks.context:
A/B testing is how data-driven companies make product decisions. Instead of debating which version of a feature is better, you run both versions simultaneously, collect data, and let statistics decide. A BI analyst's job in an A/B test: design the experiment correctly, analyse the results without bias, and communicate findings clearly.

The most common A/B testing mistakes are not statistical, they are design mistakes: running the test too short, stopping when you first see significance, testing too many variants simultaneously, and not defining the primary metric before the test starts. These mistakes produce false positives that lead companies to ship worse products.

This week you learn the statistics of A/B testing (two-sample tests, power analysis, sample size calculation) and how to run and analyse experiments using Python. You also learn the business side: how to communicate results to stakeholders who don't understand p-values.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## A/B testing: how data-driven companies decide

Instead of arguing about which button colour, headline, or price is better, data-driven companies **run both and let the data decide**. That is an A/B test: split users randomly into version A (control) and version B (variant), measure a metric, and use statistics to judge whether B truly beat A or it was just luck. It is the cleanest way to establish *causation* (last week's holy grail), because randomisation removes the confounders.

A BI analyst's role across a test: help **design** it (what to measure, how many users, how long), **monitor** it, and **analyse** the result honestly (did it really win?). This is high-value, product, growth, and marketing teams lean on analysts who can run experiments rigorously.

This week is the rigorous core: the hypothesis-testing framework, the two tests you will actually use (t-test for averages, chi-square for rates), the concepts that stop you fooling yourself (power, sample size, Type I/II errors), and how real A/B tests run and fail.

The mindset: an A/B test is a structured way to *not fool yourself*. A 4.0% to 4.3% conversion bump looks like a win, but with small samples it is often noise. The whole apparatus this week exists to answer one question honestly: "is this difference real, or did I get lucky?"

Today, orient: write a concrete test you could imagine for an e-commerce site (e.g. "does a free-shipping banner increase conversion?"), and name the control, the variant, the one metric you would measure, and your gut guess. You will learn to judge that test properly this week.

items.title: Hypothesis testing framework
items.body:
## The hypothesis-testing framework

Every A/B test (and most statistical claims) runs on the same five-step logic. Learn the frame and the specific tests become plug-ins.

1. **State two hypotheses.** The **null (H0)**: "there is no real difference", B is the same as A; any gap is chance. The **alternative (H1)**: "there is a real difference." You always test *against* the null, you assume no effect until the data is strong enough to reject that.
2. **Choose a significance level (alpha),** usually **0.05.** This is the risk you accept of falsely declaring a difference when none exists (a false positive). 0.05 means "I'll accept a 5% chance of crying wolf."
3. **Collect data and compute a test statistic** (the t-test or chi-square test pick the right one).
4. **Get the p-value.** The p-value is the probability of seeing a result *this extreme or more* **if the null were true** (if there were really no difference). Small p = the data would be very surprising under "no effect", so the null looks wrong.
5. **Decide.** If **p < alpha (e.g. p < 0.05)**, reject the null, the result is "statistically significant", B likely really differs from A. If p >= 0.05, you *fail to reject* the null, not "proven no difference", just "not enough evidence."

The two phrases that mark someone who actually understands this:
- A p-value is **not** "the probability B is better." It is the probability of the data given no effect. Subtle but important, and a classic interview gotcha.
- "Statistically significant" means "unlikely to be chance", it does **not** mean "big" or "important." A trivial 0.1% lift can be significant with millions of users (that is **practical** vs **statistical** significance, always report both).

Today, take yesterday's test idea and write it out in this five-step frame: H0, H1, alpha = 0.05, the metric, and what a "p < 0.05" conclusion would and would not let you claim.

items.title: t-test
items.body:
## The t-test: comparing two averages

Use a **t-test** when your metric is a **continuous average** and you are comparing two groups, "did average order value differ between A and B?", "is mean session length higher for the new design?"

What it does: it compares the two groups' means *relative to their variability and sample size*. A big difference in means with low variability and large samples gives a large t-statistic and a small p-value (significant). The same difference in means with high variability or tiny samples gives a small t and large p (not significant), because the gap could easily be noise. That is the whole intuition: **a difference is convincing only relative to the noise and the sample size.**

The variant you will almost always want is the **two-sample (independent) t-test** (groups A and B are different users). (A paired t-test is for before/after on the *same* units.)

You will not compute it by hand. In practice:
- **Python:** `from scipy import stats; stats.ttest_ind(group_a, group_b)` returns the t-statistic and p-value in one line.
- **Excel:** `T.TEST(arrayA, arrayB, 2, 2)`.
- Read the p-value against 0.05.

**The assumptions to respect** (so you do not misuse it): the data should be roughly normal *or* samples large enough for the central limit theorem to kick in (last week's payoff), and for the standard test, similar variances (Welch's t-test, scipy's `equal_var=False`, handles unequal variances and is a safe default). For heavily skewed data with small samples, a t-test on the mean can mislead, consider a median-based or non-parametric test.

Today, simulate or take two groups of order values from Superstore (e.g. two regions, or split randomly), run a two-sample t-test in Python or Excel, and interpret the p-value: significant difference in average order value, or not?

items.title: Chi-square test for categorical data (conversion rates, user behaviour)
items.body:
## The chi-square test: comparing rates and categories

Most A/B tests do **not** measure an average, they measure a **rate**: conversion rate, click-through rate, signup rate, did the user convert, yes/no. For comparing rates or any categorical counts, the right tool is the **chi-square test** (specifically the chi-square test of independence), not the t-test.

What it does: it checks whether the counts in a category table differ more than chance would explain. You build a contingency table:

```
            Converted   Not converted
Version A      120          2380
Version B      155          2345
```
Chi-square compares the **observed** counts to the counts you would **expect if version made no difference**, and produces a statistic and a p-value. Small p = the conversion rates differ more than chance, B's rate is really different.

When to use which, the distinction that matters:
- **Metric is a per-user number you average** (order value, time on site) -> **t-test**.
- **Metric is a rate / yes-no / category counts** (conversion, click, churn) -> **chi-square** (or a two-proportion z-test, equivalent for 2x2).

In practice:
- **Python:** `from scipy import stats; stats.chi2_contingency([[120,2380],[155,2345]])` returns the statistic, p-value, and expected counts.
- Read p against 0.05.

A caution: chi-square needs reasonable counts per cell (a rule of thumb: expected counts >= 5). With tiny conversion numbers, results are unreliable, which is exactly why sample size (tomorrow) matters so much for rate-based tests.

Today, build a 2x2 conversion table (real or simulated) and run `chi2_contingency`. State the conversion rate for A and B, the p-value, and your honest conclusion, and note you chose chi-square *because the metric is a rate*.

days.summary: Focus: Statistical power, sample size calculation, Type I and Type II errors

items.title: Statistical power, sample size calculation, Type I and Type II errors
items.body:
## Power, sample size, and the two ways to be wrong

This is the day that separates people who *run* A/B tests from people who *trust* them. Two ways a test can fool you:

- **Type I error (false positive):** you declare a winner that is not real. Its rate is **alpha** (0.05), you accept a 5% chance of this by choosing that significance level.
- **Type II error (false negative):** there *is* a real effect but your test misses it. Its rate is **beta**.

**Statistical power = 1 − beta** = the probability your test *detects* a real effect of a given size. The standard target is **80% power.** Low power is the silent killer of A/B tests: an underpowered test that comes back "not significant" tells you almost nothing, you cannot conclude "no effect", only "I didn't have enough data to see one."

**Power depends on four things, locked together:** sample size, effect size (how big a difference you want to detect), alpha, and power. Fix any three and the fourth is determined. The practical use is **sample size calculation up front:** before running, you decide "I want 80% power to detect at least a 0.5 percentage-point lift at alpha 0.05", and a calculator tells you how many users per group you need. (Python: `statsmodels` power functions; or any online A/B sample-size calculator.)

This prevents the two cardinal sins:
- **Running too small** -> underpowered -> inconclusive waste of time.
- **"Peeking" and stopping early** when you see significance -> inflates false positives badly. Decide the sample size and duration in advance and run the whole test. Stopping the moment p dips below 0.05 is how teams ship "winners" that are noise.

Today, use a sample-size calculator: for a baseline 4% conversion, a target detectable lift to 4.5%, alpha 0.05, power 0.80, find how many users per group you need (you will likely be surprised how large it is). Then state how long that test must run given a realistic daily traffic number. That calculation is exactly what a team will ask you to produce before a test.

items.title: A/B testing in practice
items.body:
## A/B testing in practice (and how it goes wrong)

The statistics are the easy part; running a trustworthy test in the messy real world is where analysts earn their keep. The end-to-end flow:

1. **Form a hypothesis tied to a metric.** "Adding free-shipping messaging will raise checkout conversion." One primary metric, decided in advance.
2. **Calculate sample size and duration** (yesterday), *before* launch. Run at least one to two full weeks to cover weekday/weekend cycles.
3. **Randomly assign** users to A/B, and check the split is actually balanced and random.
4. **Run the whole test, do not peek-and-stop.** Let it reach the planned sample.
5. **Analyse with the right test** (t-test for averages, chi-square for rates), report the lift, the p-value, *and* a confidence interval, and judge practical significance, is the effect big enough to matter, not just significant?
6. **Decide and document**, including "no significant difference" results, which are valuable (they stop you shipping useless changes).

The real-world traps a good analyst guards against:
- **Peeking** and early stopping (inflates false positives), covered, and the most common sin.
- **The multiple-comparisons problem:** test 20 metrics and ~1 will look "significant" by chance at alpha 0.05. Pre-register one primary metric; treat the rest as exploratory.
- **Novelty and seasonality effects:** a new design spikes because it is new, or a test spans a holiday. Run long enough; be wary of short windows.
- **Sample ratio mismatch:** if your 50/50 split arrives as 55/45, the randomisation or logging is broken, trust nothing until you fix it.
- **Simpson's paradox:** an effect that reverses when you split by segment. Check key segments, not just the overall number.

Today, write a one-page **A/B test plan** for your free-shipping (or chosen) hypothesis: the metric, the chosen test (and why), the sample size and duration from yesterday, and a short "threats to validity" list naming which traps above you would watch for. That plan is exactly the deliverable a product team expects from their analyst.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Ship it

Package the week into an **A/B test analysis** artefact, the thing that proves you can run an experiment end to end, not just read about it.

Produce (in Python/notebook or a documented spreadsheet + write-up):
- **A test design:** hypothesis, H0/H1, primary metric, the chosen test with justification (t-test vs chi-square), alpha, and the up-front sample-size calculation.
- **A worked analysis** on real or simulated A/B data: the contingency table or group arrays, the test run (`chi2_contingency` or `ttest_ind`), the p-value, the lift, and a confidence interval.
- **An honest conclusion:** significant or not, *and* whether the effect is practically meaningful, plus one "threat to validity" you checked.

Commit with a README framing: "An end-to-end A/B test design and analysis, demonstrating hypothesis testing, correct test selection, power/sample-size reasoning, and honest interpretation."

```
git add ab-test/ && git commit -m "BI: A/B test design + analysis (hypothesis testing, power, chi-square/t-test)"
git push
```

This is a standout portfolio piece, experimentation is exactly what growth and product teams hire BI/analytics people for, and most candidates cannot do it rigorously. Be ready to explain in an interview why you picked your test, how you sized it, and why you did not stop early. Next week: KPIs, metric design, and data storytelling, turning correct analysis into something stakeholders actually act on.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Type I and Type II errors are the two ways a hypothesis test can fool you, and naming them is less useful than feeling their cost. A Type I error (false positive) is concluding there is an effect when there is not, in an A/B test, declaring the new button a winner and shipping it, when really it does nothing. A Type II error (false negative) is missing a real effect, killing a genuinely better variant because the test did not reach significance. Which hurts more depends entirely on the cost of the action: if shipping the change is cheap and reversible, a Type I error is survivable; if shipping it means a costly engineering commitment or a risk to revenue, a false positive is the expensive one. The skill is reasoning about consequences, not just probabilities. For a checkout-flow A/B test, tell me which error you would fear more and why.

weeks.title: KPIs, Metrics Design, and Data Storytelling
weeks.context:
A KPI (Key Performance Indicator) is a metric that measures progress toward a specific business objective. Most companies have too many KPIs, and most of them are vanity metrics, numbers that look good but don't tell you whether the business is healthy or how to improve it.

Good metrics have three properties: they are actionable (someone can change their behaviour based on them), they are comparable (you can tell if this week's number is good or bad by comparing to something), and they are understandable (the person being measured understands how the number is calculated).

Data storytelling is the practice of presenting data in a narrative that leads to a decision. The best BI analysts don't just produce charts, they answer "so what?" and "now what?". This week you learn both: how to design metrics that matter, and how to present them in a way that drives action.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## From correct numbers to numbers people act on

For ten weeks you built a Superstore report that is *correct*: a clean star schema, trustworthy DAX measures, row-level security, scheduled refresh. That is the hard half. This week is the half that gets analysts promoted, turning a correct report into one that **drives a decision**.

Here is the uncomfortable truth: a technically perfect dashboard that nobody acts on is a failed dashboard. Stakeholders do not reward DAX elegance. They reward "you showed me the Central region's margin is bleeding and told me which sub-category to cut." That is the job.

This week has two halves. First, **metric design**, choosing *which* numbers belong on the dashboard. Most dashboards drown in vanity metrics that go up and to the right but never inform a decision. You will learn to separate a metric from a KPI from a North Star, and to design metrics that are actionable, comparable, and understandable.

Second, **data storytelling**, presenting those numbers as a narrative that ends in a recommendation. You will learn narrative structure (situation, insight, action), how to pick the right chart for the message, and how colour, type, and layout direct a reader's eye.

Today, orient: open your Superstore report and look at it as a stranger would. Write down, in your Notion "story" page, the single most important decision this report should help someone make. Then count how many of your current visuals actually serve that decision. Most people find half their charts are noise. That gap is what this week closes.

items.title: KPI design principles
items.body:
## What makes a metric worth tracking

A KPI, a Key Performance Indicator, is a metric tied to a specific business objective. The trap is that *anything* countable can be a metric, so dashboards fill with numbers that look busy and decide nothing. Your job is to keep the few that matter.

A good metric has three properties. **Actionable:** someone can change their behaviour based on it. "Total page views" fails this, what do you *do* differently when it moves? "Cart-abandonment rate by step" passes, it points at a fix. **Comparable:** you can tell whether today's value is good or bad, because you have a benchmark, a target, last period, or a segment to compare against. A number with no comparison is trivia. **Understandable:** the person being measured can explain how it is calculated. A KPI nobody trusts because the formula is a black box gets ignored.

## Leading vs lagging

Two flavours matter. A **lagging indicator** reports an outcome that already happened, last quarter's profit, churn this month. It is accurate but you cannot change it. A **leading indicator** predicts a future outcome, trial-to-paid conversion, sales-pipeline coverage, and you *can* still influence it. Mature dashboards pair them: the lagging KPI for accountability, the leading KPI for steering.

## On the Superstore report

Apply this now. "Total Sales" is a lagging, weakly actionable headline, fine as context, useless as a steering wheel. A sharper pair: **Profit Margin %** (lagging, accountable) alongside **discount depth on low-margin sub-categories** (leading, you can stop discounting tomorrow). Pick your report's three real KPIs and demote the rest to supporting detail. Fewer, sharper numbers beats a wall of gauges every time.

days.summary: Focus: The North Star metric framework and OKRs (Objectives and Key Results)

items.title: The North Star metric framework and OKRs (Objectives and Key Results)
items.body:
## One number above all the others

Most teams track dozens of metrics and, in a crisis, cannot agree which one matters. The **North Star metric** fixes that: it is the single number that best captures the value your product delivers to customers, the one you would optimise if you could only watch one. For Spotify it is time spent listening; for an Airbnb, nights booked. It aligns everyone, because every team can ask "does my work move the North Star?"

Beneath the North Star sit **input metrics**, the handful of levers that actually drive it. If the North Star is "nights booked", inputs might be host supply, search-to-booking conversion, and repeat-booking rate. The discipline is the tree: one North Star, a few inputs each team owns, and tactical metrics below those. Lose the tree and you are back to a wall of disconnected gauges.

## OKRs: the goal-setting frame around the metrics

OKRs, Objectives and Key Results, are how teams turn metrics into quarterly goals. The **Objective** is a qualitative, motivating aim ("Make the Central region profitable again"). The **Key Results** are 2 to 4 measurable outcomes that prove you hit it ("Lift Central margin from 6% to 11%", "Cut sub-categories with negative margin from 5 to 1"). Key Results are *outcomes*, not tasks, "ship a new dashboard" is a task and does not belong.

## On the Superstore report

Frame your report around one Objective. "Restore Superstore's overall profitability" with Key Results on margin %, negative-margin sub-categories, and discount discipline gives every visual a job: it either tracks a Key Result or it is cut. A dashboard built around an OKR practically designs itself.

items.title: Narrative structure for data presentations
items.body:
## A dashboard is an argument, not a gallery

The weakest BI work dumps every chart on one page and lets the viewer "explore". The strongest leads them through a **narrative** that ends in a recommendation. The frame that travels everywhere is three beats: **Situation, Insight, Action**, sometimes called SCR (Situation, Complication, Resolution) in consulting.

**Situation:** the shared context, the thing everyone already agrees is true. "Superstore revenue is up 12% year over year." You open here so nobody is defensive; you are stating reality.

**Insight:** the tension, the surprising or uncomfortable fact your analysis uncovered. "But profit is *flat*, because the Central region's margin collapsed from 14% to 6% on heavy discounting." This is the moment the audience leans in, growth without profit is a problem they did not see.

**Action:** the "now what". "Cap discounts on Tables and Bookcases in Central; the model says that recovers roughly 4 margin points." You end by telling them what to *do*, not by trailing off into more charts.

## Pyramid principle

Lead with the answer, then support it, the opposite of a school essay that builds to a conclusion. Executives want the recommendation in the first ten seconds, then the evidence if they choose to dig. Put your headline insight and recommendation at the top of the page; push the detailed breakdowns below the fold.

## On the Superstore report

Write the three beats for your report in your Notion "story" page as plain sentences before touching a single visual. If you cannot state the Insight and Action in two sentences, no amount of charting will rescue the dashboard, the thinking is not finished yet.

items.title: Chart selection guide
items.body:
## Pick the chart for the message, not the data type

Chart choice is not decoration, it is part of the argument. The question is never "what does this data allow?" but "what do I want the reader to *see*?" A handful of pairings cover most BI work.

**Comparison across categories** (sales by region, margin by sub-category): a **bar chart**, horizontal if the labels are long. Bars are the workhorse, accurate, instantly readable, hard to misread. Reach for them by default.

**Change over time** (monthly revenue, margin trend): a **line chart**. Lines say "this is a continuous story"; do not use them for unordered categories.

**Part-to-whole** (share of sales by category): be careful. A pie chart works only with 2 to 4 slices; beyond that, a **stacked bar** or just a ranked bar with shares labelled reads far better. Most pies should have been bars.

**Relationship** (discount vs profit): a **scatter plot**, the single best way to expose "higher discounts are dragging margin down", because the eye sees the downward cloud immediately.

**Single key number** (current margin vs target): a **card** or KPI visual, big number, small context. Do not bury your headline KPI inside a chart.

## Anti-patterns to refuse

Dual-axis charts that imply a correlation the data does not support; 3-D anything (it distorts the values); donut charts used as decoration; and the "everything on one axis" mess. When a chart needs a legend with eight colours, the chart has failed.

## On the Superstore report

Audit every visual against its message. The discount-vs-profit story almost certainly wants a scatter you do not yet have, and at least one of your pies probably wants to become a ranked bar. Swap them, and watch the argument get sharper.

days.title: Colour, typography, and layout in data visualisation design
days.summary: Focus: Colour, typography, and layout in data visualisation design

items.title: Colour, typography, and layout in data visualisation design
items.body:
## Design directs the eye, whether you plan it or not

Every dashboard makes design choices; the only question is whether you made them on purpose. Three levers, colour, typography, layout, decide what a reader notices first and whether they trust the result.

## Colour: meaning, not mood

Use colour to encode information, never to "brighten things up". Pick one **accent colour** for the thing you want noticed (the KPI that is off target) and render everything else in muted greys. A dashboard where every chart is a different rainbow has no focal point, so the eye gives up. Reserve **red and green for genuinely good/bad** semantics (and add a shape or label, because ~8% of men are red-green colour-blind, colour alone is not accessible). Use a **sequential** scale (light-to-dark of one hue) for magnitude, and a **diverging** scale (two hues from a neutral midpoint) only for above/below-target data.

## Typography: hierarchy

Two type sizes minimum, a clear hierarchy: big bold numbers for KPIs, a readable size for labels, smaller for footnotes and sources. Left-align text, right-align numbers (so digits line up and you can compare magnitudes at a glance). One font family is plenty.

## Layout: the Z and the grid

Western readers scan in a **Z / F pattern**, top-left first. Put your most important KPI top-left, the supporting trend top-right, detail below. Align everything to a **grid**, ragged edges read as careless and quietly erode trust. Leave whitespace; a cramped dashboard feels harder than it is.

## On the Superstore report

Restyle one page: greys for context, a single accent for the off-target margin KPI, KPIs top-left, consistent number formatting, aligned to a grid. Screenshot before and after, the difference in how fast someone "gets it" is the whole lesson.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Metric, KPI, and North Star metric are three nested levels of importance, and using the words loosely makes a strategy conversation mushy. A metric is any number you can measure, page views, signups, email opens; there are thousands. A KPI (Key Performance Indicator) is the small subset of metrics you have decided actually indicate success against a goal, the ones you put on the dashboard and hold people to. A North Star metric is the single number that best captures the core value your product delivers and that the whole company rallies behind, for a SaaS company, perhaps 'weekly active teams' or 'monthly recurring revenue'. The hierarchy is: many metrics, few KPIs, one North Star. Give me an example of each for a SaaS business, and explain why elevating the wrong metric to North Star could steer the whole company astray.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## When Power BI is not enough

Python is not a replacement for Power BI, it is what you reach for when Power BI runs out of room. Power BI is brilliant at modelling, fast aggregation, and interactive dashboards. It is awkward at messy multi-step data cleaning, custom statistics, reproducible analysis you can hand to someone else, and anything you want to run on a schedule without a person clicking refresh. That is Python's territory.

For a BI analyst, the Python toolkit is small and specific: **pandas** for manipulating tabular data (think SQL plus Excel in code), **matplotlib/seaborn** for quick exploratory plots, and **Jupyter notebooks** as the place you do and share the work. You are not building production software. You are writing analysis scripts, reviewable, rerunnable, and modifiable, which is exactly what makes them more trustworthy than a spreadsheet someone hand-edited.

This week you learn the pandas operations that show up constantly in real BI work: reading data, selecting and filtering, `groupby` for aggregation, `merge` for joins, `pivot_table` for cross-tabs, and resampling time series. These map almost one-to-one onto things you already do in Power Query and DAX, so you are translating skills, not starting over.

The mental model: a pandas **DataFrame** is a table, rows and named columns, just like a Power BI table or a SQL result. Everything this week is "do to a DataFrame what you already do to a Power BI table, but in code you can save, diff, and rerun."

Today, orient: load your exported Superstore CSV into a DataFrame with `pd.read_csv`, and run `.head()`, `.shape`, and `.info()`. Write one sentence on what each tells you. You have just done in three lines what the Power BI field pane shows you visually.

items.title: Python setup
items.body:
## The environment, then the language

Before pandas, get fluent in the workspace, because friction here is what makes people quit. In **Jupyter Lab** you write code in **cells** and run a cell with Shift+Enter. Output appears directly below: a number, a table, a chart. This tight loop, write a line, see the result, adjust, is why notebooks beat scripts for exploration.

Two habits keep notebooks sane. First, **run cells top to bottom**; a notebook where you jump around becomes a state nobody can reproduce, including you tomorrow. When in doubt, "Restart Kernel and Run All", if it survives that, it is reproducible. Second, **keep imports at the top**: `import pandas as pd`, `import numpy as np`, `import matplotlib.pyplot as plt`. The `as pd` is an alias everyone uses; matching the convention makes your code readable to any analyst.

## The Python you actually need

You do not need deep computer science for BI. You need: **variables** (`sales = 1500`), **lists** (`['East','West']`), **dictionaries** (`{'region':'East','sales':1500}`, the shape of one row), a **for loop** to repeat work, and **functions** to name a reusable step. That covers most analysis code. Resist the urge to learn classes, decorators, and async, they are production-software concerns, not BI ones.

## Virtual environments, briefly

Keep each project's packages isolated with `python -m venv .venv` (or a conda env). It prevents the "it worked last month and now it is broken" mess when one project upgrades pandas and breaks another. Activate it, install into it, and commit a `requirements.txt` so the environment is reproducible.

Today: in a fresh notebook, create a dictionary representing one Superstore order, put three of them in a list, and loop over it to print each region. Small, but it is the exact pattern under every DataFrame.

items.title: pandas fundamentals
items.body:
## The DataFrame is the whole game

pandas gives you one object you will use all day: the **DataFrame**, a table with labelled rows (the index) and named columns. Get data in, look at it, select parts, and you are most of the way there.

**Reading data:** `df = pd.read_csv('superstore.csv')`. There are `read_excel`, `read_sql`, and more, but CSV is the workhorse. Immediately inspect: `.head()` (first rows), `.shape` (rows, columns), `.info()` (column names, types, null counts), `.describe()` (summary stats for numbers). These four are your "what did I just load?" reflex.

**Selecting columns:** `df['Sales']` gets one column (a Series); `df[['Region','Sales']]` gets several (a DataFrame). The double brackets trip everyone up once, single = one column as a Series, list inside = a DataFrame.

**Filtering rows** uses boolean masks, the single most important pandas idea. `df[df['Region'] == 'Central']` keeps Central rows. Combine conditions with `&` and `|` (and wrap each in parentheses): `df[(df['Region']=='Central') & (df['Profit'] < 0)]` finds Central's loss-making orders, the exact "where is the margin bleeding?" question from your storytelling week, now answerable in one line.

**Creating columns:** `df['Margin'] = df['Profit'] / df['Sales']`. Vectorised, the operation runs across the whole column at once, no loop. This is both faster and clearer than looping, and it is how pandas is meant to be used.

Today: load Superstore, filter to negative-profit orders, add a `Margin` column, and sort by it ascending with `.sort_values('Margin')`. You have just reproduced a DAX-and-filter exploration in four readable, rerunnable lines.

items.title: Data manipulation
items.body:
## Aggregating and combining: groupby, merge, pivot

Filtering finds rows; the real BI work is summarising and joining. Three operations cover most of it, and each maps onto something you already know.

**groupby** is "GROUP BY from SQL". `df.groupby('Region')['Sales'].sum()` gives sales per region; `df.groupby('Region').agg({'Sales':'sum','Profit':'mean','Order ID':'nunique'})` computes several aggregates at once. The pattern is always: split by a key, apply a function, combine the results. If you can write the GROUP BY, you can write the groupby.

**merge** is a SQL join. `pd.merge(orders, returns, on='Order ID', how='left')` attaches return info to each order. The `how` matters: `inner` keeps only matches, `left` keeps all orders (and fills missing returns with NaN), exactly the join-type decisions you made building the Superstore model. Getting `how` wrong is the most common source of "my totals changed", so name it explicitly.

**pivot_table** is the Excel pivot in code. `df.pivot_table(index='Region', columns='Category', values='Sales', aggfunc='sum')` gives a region-by-category grid of sales. Great for a quick cross-tab you would otherwise build by hand.

**apply** runs a custom function per row or column when no built-in fits, `df['Tier'] = df['Sales'].apply(lambda x: 'High' if x > 1000 else 'Low')`. Use it sparingly; a vectorised expression or `np.where` is faster when it exists, but `apply` is your escape hatch for logic too custom for built-ins.

Today: from Superstore, build a region-by-category `pivot_table` of total profit, then `groupby('Sub-Category')` to find the three sub-categories with the worst total margin. That is a board-level finding produced in two cells.

items.title: Data cleaning with pandas
items.body:
## Real data is dirty, and cleaning it is the job

Textbook datasets are tidy. Real exports are not: missing values, duplicate rows, text where numbers should be, inconsistent labels ("Central", "central", "CEN"). Most of an analyst's pandas time is cleaning, and doing it *in code* beats hand-editing a spreadsheet because every fix is recorded, reviewable, and rerunnable on next month's data.

**Missing values:** find them with `df.isna().sum()` per column. Then decide, deliberately, what each gap *means*. Drop rows only when the missing field is essential (`df.dropna(subset=['Sales'])`). Fill when a sensible default exists (`df['Discount'].fillna(0)`). Never blanket-`fillna(0)` numeric columns without thinking, a missing profit is not zero profit, and pretending it is corrupts every downstream total.

**Duplicates:** `df.duplicated().sum()` counts them; `df.drop_duplicates()` removes them. Watch for *partial* duplicates, the same order ID appearing twice because a join fanned out, which inflate totals silently. This is the same trap that breaks a Power BI measure when a relationship is wrong.

**Types:** a column read as text will not sum. `pd.to_datetime(df['Order Date'])` and `pd.to_numeric(df['Sales'], errors='coerce')` fix the two most common cases. `errors='coerce'` turns un-parseable values into NaN so you can find and inspect them rather than crashing.

**Consistency:** standardise text with `df['Region'].str.strip().str.title()` so "central " and "Central" stop being two groups. Inconsistent categories are why a groupby sometimes shows a region twice.

Today: take a deliberately messy slice of Superstore (or inject some nulls and dupes), and write a cleaning cell that documents each decision in a comment. A reviewer should be able to read *why* you dropped, filled, or recast each column, that audit trail is the point.

items.title: Basic matplotlib and seaborn for quick EDA plots
items.body:
## Plotting to think, not to present

In Python you make two kinds of charts. **Exploratory** plots are fast and ugly, made to *understand* the data for yourself. **Explanatory** plots are polished, made to *communicate*, and for those you would usually go back to Power BI or Looker Studio. This week is about the first kind: quick EDA plots that answer "what does this look like?" in seconds.

**matplotlib** is the foundation. `df['Sales'].hist()` shows a distribution; `df.plot(x='Order Date', y='Sales')` a line; `df.plot.scatter(x='Discount', y='Profit')` a relationship. pandas wraps matplotlib so most plots are one method call straight off a DataFrame.

**seaborn** sits on top and makes statistical plots prettier with less code. `sns.boxplot(data=df, x='Region', y='Profit')` instantly shows the spread and outliers per region, the discount-driven losses jump out as the long lower whiskers. `sns.heatmap(df.corr(numeric_only=True), annot=True)` shows which numeric columns move together. `sns.scatterplot` with a `hue=` colours points by a category, so the discount-vs-profit cloud can be split by region in one line.

The discipline: a plot during analysis is a question, not a deliverable. Make it, read it, move on, do not spend twenty minutes styling a chart you are using to think. Title it, glance, decide, next.

Today: on Superstore, make three EDA plots, a histogram of profit, a boxplot of profit by region, and a scatter of discount vs profit coloured by category. Write one sentence under each on what it told you. The scatter should make the "discounts are killing Central's margin" story undeniable, the same insight, now reached in code you can rerun next month.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Ship it

Package the week into a **reproducible analysis notebook**, the artefact that proves you can take a raw export and turn it into findings without a single manual spreadsheet edit.

Produce a Jupyter notebook that:
- **Loads** the Superstore CSV and inspects it (`head`, `shape`, `info`).
- **Cleans** it with documented decisions, types fixed, nulls and duplicates handled, text standardised, each step explained in a comment.
- **Analyses** it: at least one `groupby`, one `merge` (e.g. orders to returns), and one `pivot_table`, ending in a concrete finding (your worst-margin sub-categories).
- **Visualises** the key finding with 2 to 3 EDA plots that support the story.
- **Concludes** in a markdown cell: the analytical question, the answer, and the recommendation.

Commit it with a README:

```
git add bi-python/ && git commit -m "BI: reproducible pandas analysis of Superstore (clean, groupby/merge/pivot, EDA)"
git push
```

This is a strong portfolio piece precisely because it is reproducible, "Restart and Run All" regenerates every number, which is exactly the trust a spreadsheet cannot offer. In an interview, be ready to explain why you cleaned each column the way you did; that judgment is what separates an analyst from someone who just calls `.mean()`.

Next week: cloud BI with BigQuery and Looker Studio, moving from files on your laptop to a warehouse and dashboards that live at a URL.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: groupby().agg() and pivot_table() in pandas both summarise data, but they shape the output differently, and choosing the right one saves you a reshaping headache. groupby().agg() collapses rows into groups and returns a long, tidy result, one row per group, columns for your aggregations, which is ideal when you are feeding the result into more code or a chart. pivot_table() reshapes into a spreadsheet-style grid, spreading one variable across the columns, closer to what you would build in Excel, ideal for a human-readable cross-tab (sales by region down the side, by year across the top). pivot_table also handles aggregation and missing combinations gracefully. So: groupby for tidy, code-friendly summaries; pivot_table for grid-shaped, presentation-friendly cross-tabs. Give me one analysis where pivot_table is clearly the better choice and one where groupby().agg() is, and explain the difference in the shape you get back.

weeks.title: Cloud BI: Google Looker Studio and BigQuery
weeks.context:
Cloud BI tools, Google Looker Studio, AWS QuickSight, Tableau Cloud, have a different architecture from desktop tools like Power BI Desktop. Data lives in a cloud warehouse (BigQuery, Redshift, Snowflake), queries run in the cloud, and reports are web-based and collaborative. There is no .pbix file to email, the report is a URL.

BigQuery is Google's managed data warehouse and one of the best places to learn cloud BI because it has a free tier with 1TB of query processing per month. Looker Studio (formerly Google Data Studio) connects to BigQuery natively and is free. Together they give you a production-grade cloud BI stack at zero cost.

The key difference from desktop BI: in cloud BI, your data stays in the warehouse and you query it live (DirectQuery equivalent). This means SQL skills matter more, every visualisation is a SQL query under the hood.

## What it is
This week's stack is entirely Google's cloud: a **Google Cloud Platform (GCP)** account, **BigQuery** (the managed data warehouse where your data lives and queries run), and **Looker Studio** (the free, web-based dashboard tool that connects to it). Together they are a production-grade cloud BI stack that costs nothing on the free tier.

## What you'll do today
- Create a Google Cloud account (a credit card is required for verification, but the free tier is generous: 1 TB of query processing and 10 GB of storage per month)

## Why before anything else
Cloud BI has more moving parts than a desktop tool, accounts, projects, billing, permissions. Untangle those today, on a trivial query, so the rest of the week is about BI, not Google Cloud paperwork.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## The architecture shift: from files to a warehouse

Everything so far lived on your machine, a `.pbix` file, a CSV, a notebook. Cloud BI breaks that model, and understanding why is the point of the week. In a cloud stack, **the data lives in a warehouse** (BigQuery), **queries run in the cloud** on Google's hardware, and **reports are URLs**, not files you email. Nobody passes around a `dashboard_final_v3.pbix`; everyone opens the same live link.

This changes three things. **Scale:** BigQuery scans terabytes in seconds because the work runs across thousands of machines, your laptop's RAM stops being the ceiling. **Collaboration:** the report is a single shared source of truth, edited live, with no "which version is current?" confusion. **Freshness:** the dashboard queries the warehouse directly, so it reflects the data as it stands, no manual refresh-and-republish.

The trade-off is a new mental model. In Power BI Desktop you *imported* data and the model lived inside the file. In cloud BI, **the warehouse is the model**: your tables and the SQL that shapes them live in BigQuery, and Looker Studio is a thin presentation layer on top. The centre of gravity moves from the dashboard tool to the warehouse. Get the SQL and the tables right, and the dashboard is easy; get them wrong, and no amount of chart polish saves you.

There is also a cost dimension that desktop tools never had: BigQuery bills by **data scanned per query**, so a careless `SELECT *` on a huge table can cost real money. You will learn to write queries that scan less, the cloud-BI version of performance tuning.

Today, orient: load your Superstore CSV into a BigQuery table (the console has a simple upload), and run `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM your_table`. You have just moved your project from a file on your laptop to a cloud warehouse, the same data, a completely different architecture.

items.title: Google Cloud Platform basics
items.body:
## Just enough GCP to be dangerous

Google Cloud is vast, hundreds of services, but a BI analyst needs a small, specific corner of it. Learn these five ideas and the console stops being intimidating.

**Projects** are the top-level container. Every resource, every dataset, every dollar of billing belongs to exactly one project. Use one project per real-world initiative so costs and access are cleanly separated. The **project ID** is the globally unique name you will reference in SQL and connections.

**Billing** attaches to a project. The free tier covers far more than a learner will use, but set a **budget alert** anyway (Billing → Budgets) so a runaway query emails you instead of surprising you. This is a professional habit, not paranoia.

**IAM (Identity and Access Management)** controls who can do what. The core concept is the **role**: you grant a person (or service account) a role like "BigQuery Data Viewer" on a project. The discipline is **least privilege**, give the narrowest role that does the job. An analyst usually needs "BigQuery User" (run queries) and "Data Viewer" (read tables), not "Owner".

**Datasets** in BigQuery are like schemas or folders, they group related tables. **Service accounts** are non-human identities that let a scheduled job authenticate without a person logging in, you will meet them when you automate.

The instinct to resist: do not go service-hunting. You will see Pub/Sub, Dataflow, Vertex AI in the menu, ignore them. For BI, it is BigQuery plus Looker Studio, full stop.

Today: in your project, create a BigQuery **dataset** called `superstore`, and move your uploaded table into it. Then set a billing budget alert at a low threshold. You now have a clean, cost-guarded home for the week's work.

items.title: BigQuery SQL
items.body:
## BigQuery SQL: standard SQL, warehouse muscles

The good news: BigQuery uses **standard SQL**, so everything from your SQL-for-BI week, joins, GROUP BY, window functions, CTEs, works almost unchanged. The differences are about scale and cost, not syntax.

**Table references** are three-part: `` `project.dataset.table` `` in backticks. `SELECT region, SUM(sales) FROM `myproj.superstore.orders` GROUP BY region` is exactly the BI aggregation you already write, just pointed at a warehouse.

**Cost-aware querying** is the new skill. BigQuery bills by **bytes scanned**, and it scans every column you select across every row in range, *regardless of your WHERE clause filtering rows*. Two habits follow. First, **never `SELECT *`** on a wide table when you need three columns, name them, and you scan a fraction of the data. Second, if your table is **partitioned by date**, filter on the partition column (`WHERE order_date >= '2024-01-01'`) so BigQuery skips whole partitions. The console shows an estimated bytes-scanned *before* you run, treat that number as a price tag.

**Useful BigQuery extras:** `APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT()` for fast (slightly approximate) cardinality on huge tables; `SAFE_DIVIDE(profit, sales)` to get NULL instead of a divide-by-zero error; and **scheduled queries**, SQL that runs on a cron schedule and writes results to a table, which is how you pre-compute heavy aggregations so dashboards stay fast and cheap.

The pattern that matters for BI: do the heavy lifting in SQL, in the warehouse, and let the dashboard query a small, pre-aggregated result. A Looker Studio chart hitting a 10-row summary table is instant; one re-aggregating 10 million raw rows on every page load is slow and expensive.

Today: rewrite your worst-margin-sub-category analysis as a BigQuery query against the `superstore` dataset, selecting only the columns you need, and note the estimated bytes scanned. That number is the cloud-BI cost you are now responsible for.

items.title: Looker Studio (formerly Data Studio)
items.body:
## Looker Studio: the dashboard as a URL

Looker Studio (formerly Google Data Studio) is Google's free dashboarding tool, and it is the cloud counterpart to the Power BI report canvas. The shift in thinking: there is no imported model inside the report. The report is a **thin layer over a live data source**, here, your BigQuery `superstore` dataset.

**Connecting:** add a BigQuery data source and point it at a table or, better, a **custom query** (your pre-aggregated SQL from yesterday). Using a custom query means Looker Studio charts hit a small, fast result set instead of re-scanning raw data, the performance-and-cost discipline carried into the dashboard layer.

**Building** will feel familiar: drag a chart, pick a **dimension** (a category to break down by, Region) and a **metric** (a number to aggregate, Sum of Sales). The vocabulary, dimensions and metrics, is the same modelling language you have used since Power BI. Add **filter controls** and a **date-range control** so viewers can slice the report themselves, the cloud equivalent of slicers.

**Calculated fields** let you make new metrics in the report (`Profit / Sales` for margin), but the rule of thumb mirrors the warehouse lesson: compute heavy or reusable logic in **BigQuery SQL**, and keep Looker Studio calculated fields for light, presentation-level tweaks. Logic in the warehouse is shared, testable, and cheap; logic buried in a chart is none of those.

**Sharing** is the payoff: hit Share, and you get a link or an embeddable report with view/edit permissions, no file to send, no version drift. This is the collaboration promise of cloud BI made concrete.

Today: rebuild one page of your Superstore dashboard in Looker Studio on top of your BigQuery source, a KPI scorecard, a region bar chart, and the discount-vs-profit scatter, then share a view-only link. You now have the same insight, living at a URL instead of in a file.

days.summary: Focus: Scheduled reports and email delivery in Looker Studio

items.title: Scheduled reports and email delivery in Looker Studio
items.body:
## Delivery: pushing the report to people who never open it

A dashboard only creates value when the right person sees the right number at the right time. Many stakeholders will never open a BI tool, they live in email. Cloud BI closes that gap with **scheduled delivery**: Looker Studio can email a PDF snapshot of a report on a recurring schedule.

**Setting it up:** in a Looker Studio report, use **Share → Schedule delivery**. Choose recipients, a cadence (daily, weekly, the first of the month), and the pages to include. At each interval, Looker Studio renders the live report to PDF and emails it. The executive who wants "Monday-morning margins in my inbox" gets exactly that, without you touching anything.

**The two-layer freshness chain.** Scheduled *delivery* sends the report; it does not refresh the *data*. The data is fresh because BigQuery holds the latest rows, often kept current by a **scheduled query** that rebuilds your summary tables on a cron (say, 6 a.m. daily). So the real automation is a chain: scheduled query refreshes the warehouse table → Looker Studio reads it live → scheduled delivery emails the snapshot. Order matters: deliver *after* the refresh, or you mail yesterday's numbers.

**Design for the format.** A PDF in an inbox is static, no hovering, no drilling, so the emailed page must stand alone. Lead with the headline KPIs, keep it to one or two pages, and make the "so what" legible at a glance. This is the storytelling discipline from W11 meeting the constraints of email.

Today: schedule a weekly PDF of your Superstore Looker Studio report to your own address, and (if you set one up) confirm a scheduled query refreshes the underlying table first. You have now built an unattended pipeline: data refreshes, report reads it, stakeholders receive it, no human in the loop.

items.title: Think it through
items.body: What are the limitations of Looker Studio compared to Tableau and Power BI?

items.title: Intro to Looker (enterprise)
items.body:
## Looker (enterprise): why "modelled BI" exists

Confusingly, Google ships two products with similar names. **Looker Studio** (this week's tool) is the free, drag-and-drop dashboard builder. **Looker** (no "Studio") is the enterprise platform large companies pay for, and it is worth understanding even if you never touch it, because interviewers ask and the idea behind it is important.

Looker's defining feature is **LookML**, a modelling layer where analysts define dimensions, measures, and the business logic of every metric **once, in version-controlled code**. When the whole company's definition of "active customer" or "net revenue" lives in one reviewed LookML model, every report inherits the same definition. That kills the classic enterprise disease: finance and marketing presenting different "revenue" numbers in the same meeting because each rebuilt the metric their own way.

This is the **governed semantic layer** idea, and it is the enterprise answer to a problem you have already felt: metric logic scattered across dozens of dashboards drifts and disagrees. Centralise the definitions, and trust scales with the company. Power BI's answer to the same problem is shared **datasets / semantic models**; dbt's `metrics` and tools like Cube play the role elsewhere. The vocabulary differs; the principle, define metrics once, govern them, reuse everywhere, is the same.

You do not need to learn LookML now. You need to be able to say, in an interview, *why* a 5,000-person company pays for Looker when Looker Studio is free: governance and a single source of metric truth, not prettier charts.

Today: write a short note in your repo contrasting Looker Studio vs Looker, free and ungoverned vs paid and governed-by-LookML, and connect it to a real risk you have seen, two dashboards that disagree because the metric was redefined. That framing is exactly what separates a junior answer from a senior one.

## Ship it

Package the week into a **live cloud BI dashboard**, the artefact that proves you can stand up a warehouse-backed report that lives at a URL, not in a file.

- **A short README** documenting the architecture, warehouse → SQL summary → live report → delivery, and the cost habit you used (named columns, partition filters, estimated bytes scanned).

Commit the SQL and README:

```
git add cloud-bi/ && git commit -m "BI: cloud stack on BigQuery + Looker Studio (warehouse, summary SQL, shared report)"
git push
```

Showing the *same* Superstore analysis rebuilt on a cloud warehouse, with a shareable URL and cost-aware SQL, signals you understand modern BI architecture, not just a single product. In interviews, be ready to explain why you pre-aggregate in BigQuery instead of letting the dashboard re-scan raw data.

items.body: Looker Studio and Looker share a name and a parent (Google) but are very different products, and knowing why both exist tells you when to reach for each. items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## AI as an accelerator, not an analyst

AI is now embedded in every major BI platform, Power BI Copilot, Tableau Pulse, Looker's AI, plus standalone assistants like Claude and ChatGPT. Ignoring them is leaving productivity on the table. Over-trusting them is worse: it ships wrong numbers with confidence. This week is about the disciplined middle.

The core distinction: **mechanical work** vs **judgment work**. Mechanical work is writing a window-function query, translating a DAX measure, formatting a chart, drafting a summary, tedious, well-defined, and exactly what AI does well. Judgment work is deciding *which* metric matters, whether a result is trustworthy, what experiment to run, and how to tell a stakeholder something they do not want to hear. AI cannot own that, and pretending it can is how analysts get embarrassed.

So the skill is **delegation with verification**. You hand the assistant the mechanical 80%, generate this SQL, explain this error, draft this summary, and you keep the judgment 20%: does this query actually answer my question, is this number plausible, is this the right recommendation? An AI-assisted analyst is faster, not replaced; the human stays the editor-in-chief.

This reframes a fear. AI does not make BI analysts obsolete; it raises the floor. When anyone can generate a chart from a prompt, the differentiator becomes the judgment, knowing what to ask, spotting when the answer is wrong, and connecting the number to a decision. That is precisely the muscle you have spent fourteen weeks building.

Today, orient: take one real task from your Superstore project, a DAX measure or a SQL query you already wrote correctly, and ask Claude to produce it from a plain-English description. Compare its answer to your known-good version. Where it matches, that is work you can safely delegate; where it differs, that is exactly the judgment you must keep.

items.title: Prompt engineering for data analysis
items.body:
## Prompting for data work: context is everything

A vague prompt gets a vague, often wrong, answer. The single biggest lever in AI-assisted analysis is **giving the model the context it needs to be correct**. For data work, that means three things in almost every prompt.

**The schema.** The model cannot guess your column names, types, or table relationships. Paste them: "Table `orders(order_id, order_date DATE, region STRING, sales FLOAT64, profit FLOAT64, discount FLOAT64)`." With the schema, you get runnable SQL; without it, you get a plausible-looking template that references columns you do not have.

**The dialect and tool.** "Write SQL" is ambiguous, BigQuery, T-SQL, and Postgres differ. "Write **BigQuery standard SQL**" or "Write a **Power BI DAX** measure" pins it down. State the tool every time.

**The goal and constraints.** Not "analyse sales" but "find the three sub-categories with the worst total profit margin, where margin = profit / sales, excluding rows with zero sales." Specific goal, explicit formula, edge cases named.

Two reliable techniques layer on top. **Few-shot:** show one worked example of the style you want ("here is one measure I like, written this way, now write the next three to match"). And **ask for reasoning on hard problems:** "explain your approach before writing the query" surfaces a flawed plan *before* it becomes flawed code you have to debug.

The anti-pattern is treating the assistant like a search box. It is a collaborator that is brilliant when briefed and unreliable when starved of context. The five minutes you spend pasting schema and stating constraints is what turns "looks right" into "is right".

Today: write a reusable **prompt template** for your own BI work, a fill-in-the-blanks block with slots for schema, dialect/tool, goal, formula, and edge cases. Use it to generate one query against your Superstore schema, and note how much better the result is than a one-line ask.

items.title: AI-assisted SQL and DAX
items.body:
## The highest-value use: generating and debugging SQL and DAX

The fastest wins from AI in BI are in the two query languages you live in. Used well, the assistant turns "I half-remember the syntax" into working code in seconds, *as long as you verify*.

**Generating SQL.** With the schema and dialect in your prompt, ask for the query in plain English: "BigQuery SQL: monthly profit margin per region, as a 3-month moving average, ordered by region then month." You will often get a correct window-function query faster than you could type it. The verification step is non-negotiable: read the logic, then **run it and sanity-check the numbers** against a figure you already trust.

**Generating DAX.** DAX is notoriously unintuitive, exactly where AI helps most. "Power BI DAX measure: sales for the same period last year, returning blank when there is no prior-year data." You will likely get a correct `CALCULATE(... SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR ...)` pattern. But DAX has a subtle trap the model often misses: **filter context**. A measure that looks right can compute wrong totals because of how it interacts with the visual's filters. Always test a generated measure in a real visual, not just in isolation.

**Debugging.** This is where AI shines least ambiguously. Paste the broken query *and the exact error message* and ask "why does this fail and how do I fix it?" The model is excellent at parsing cryptic errors, a missing GROUP BY column, a type mismatch, an aggregation inside a window function. Pasting the full error, not your paraphrase, makes the difference.

**Explaining.** Inherit a 40-line DAX measure or a gnarly CTE chain? Paste it and ask for a plain-English, step-by-step explanation. This turns documentation archaeology into a two-minute read.

The discipline throughout: **AI writes the draft, you own the correctness.** A wrong number that ships looks exactly like a right one until someone makes a bad decision on it.

Today: take the hardest query or measure from your Superstore project, regenerate it from a plain-English prompt, then paste a deliberately broken version and have the assistant diagnose it. You are practising the two highest-frequency AI moves in real BI: generate, and debug.

items.title: Power BI Copilot and Tableau AI features
items.body:
## AI built into the BI tools themselves

Beyond general assistants, the platforms now ship their own AI, and a working analyst should know what each does and where it stops.

**Power BI Copilot** lives inside Power BI. It can draft DAX measures from a description, generate a report page from a prompt ("show sales by region over time"), and answer natural-language questions about a model ("which region had the highest margin last quarter?"). It is genuinely useful for first drafts, but it is bounded by your **model**: if relationships or measures are wrong, Copilot confidently produces wrong answers on top of them. The lesson of fourteen weeks holds, a good model is the prerequisite, and Copilot amplifies whatever you built, right or wrong.

**Tableau Pulse / AI** surfaces automated insights and natural-language summaries of metrics, "sales are down 8% week-over-week, driven by the West region", pushing analysis toward people who would never build a viz.

**Looker / Google's AI** answers natural-language questions against the governed LookML model, which is the safer pattern: AI on top of *governed* metric definitions is far more trustworthy than AI guessing at raw tables.

The common thread, and the thing to say in an interview: **these features are a presentation and drafting layer over your model, not a substitute for it.** Natural-language Q&A is only as correct as the semantic model it queries. AI does not rescue a bad model; it makes a good one faster to use. The analyst's job, building the trustworthy model and checking the AI's output, does not go away, it becomes the part that matters most.

Today: if you have Power BI Copilot access, ask it to draft a measure you already wrote and compare; if not, write a one-page note on how Power BI Copilot, Tableau Pulse, and Looker AI each relate to the underlying model, and why a wrong model makes all three dangerous. That framing is exactly what a senior interviewer is probing for.
