items.title: AI for data storytelling
items.body:
## AI for the story, where it helps and where it lies

AI is a strong drafting partner for the *communication* half of BI, and a dangerous one if you let it invent. The split: use it to **draft and tighten language**, never to **generate facts**.

**Where it genuinely helps.** Paste your real findings, the actual numbers from your analysis, and ask for a first draft of the executive summary: "Here are the results: Central margin fell from 14% to 6% on heavy discounting in Tables and Bookcases. Draft a 4-sentence summary for a non-technical VP, using the Situation-Insight-Action structure." You get a clean, well-structured draft to edit, which beats staring at a blank page. It is also good at **reframing for an audience** ("rewrite this for a finance stakeholder who cares about margin, not units"), **tightening** waffle, and **suggesting the chart** for a message.

**Where it lies, the non-negotiable rule.** Never let AI produce the *numbers* or *interpretation* from raw data it cannot actually compute. Ask it "what's interesting in this dataset?" with no real figures and it will **hallucinate plausible-sounding insights**, "sales peaked in Q3", that may be entirely false. The facts must come from *your* verified analysis; AI only helps you *phrase* them. Feed it your real, checked numbers and have it write the prose; do not ask it to invent the findings.

**The workflow that keeps you safe:** you compute and verify → you hand the assistant the confirmed facts → it drafts the narrative → you edit for accuracy and voice. The human owns every number; the AI owns none.

Today: take the real, verified findings from your storytelling-week dashboard, hand them to the assistant, and have it draft a Situation-Insight-Action executive summary. Then red-team it: check every number against your source and rewrite anything it softened, sharpened, or invented. The edit *is* the skill.

items.title: Responsible AI use
items.body:
## Responsible AI use: the lines you do not cross

AI in BI introduces real risks, and a professional analyst manages them deliberately rather than discovering them after a leak or a bad decision. Four lines matter.

**Data privacy.** Pasting data into a public AI tool may send it to a third party, and depending on the plan, it may be used for training. **Never paste real customer data, PII, financial records, or anything under NDA into a consumer AI tool.** Work with **schema and synthetic or anonymised samples** instead, the model needs the *structure* to write a query, not real social-security numbers. Where the stakes are high, use enterprise tiers with no-training, data-residency guarantees, that is a procurement decision, not a personal one.

**Hallucination.** AI states wrong answers with the same confidence as right ones. It will invent a function that does not exist, a column you never had, or an "insight" with no basis. The mitigation is structural: **verify every output, run every query, sanity-check every number** against something you trust. Treat AI output as a confident draft from a bright intern, useful, never authoritative.

**Bias and fairness.** If AI helps interpret data about people, hiring, lending, customer segmentation, it can launder bias in the data into a confident recommendation. Keep a human in the loop on any analysis that affects people, and be able to explain the *why* behind a number, not just cite that "the AI said so".

**Attribution and accountability.** *You* are accountable for what you ship, full stop. "The AI generated it" is not a defence when a wrong number drives a bad decision. Understand every query and measure you put your name on; if you cannot explain it, do not ship it.

Today: write a short **AI-use policy** for your own BI practice, what you will and won't paste, how you verify outputs, and where a human must stay in the loop. This is the kind of judgment that marks a trustworthy analyst, and exactly what a thoughtful employer wants to hear.

- **A reusable prompt library** for your BI work: templates for generating SQL, generating DAX, debugging an error, and explaining inherited code, each with slots for schema, dialect/tool, goal, and constraints.
- **A worked example** end to end: a plain-English request → the AI-generated query/measure → your verification step (run + sanity-check) → the corrected final version, with notes on what the AI got wrong.
- **An AI-drafted, human-edited executive summary** of a real finding, showing the before (AI draft) and after (your edit), with a one-line note on every fact you verified.
- **Your personal AI-use policy** from Day 6.

Commit it:

```
git add ai-bi-workflow/ && git commit -m "BI: AI-assisted workflow (prompt library, verified generate/debug, responsible use)"
git push
```

This is a forward-looking portfolio piece. Employers know AI is reshaping BI; what they cannot tell from a CV is whether you use it *responsibly*, faster on the mechanical work, rigorous on verification, honest about its limits. This artefact shows exactly that judgment, which is rarer and more valuable than the speed itself.

Next week: BI portfolio and interview preparation, packaging everything you have built into proof of work that gets you the interview.

items.body: The honest answer to 'what should AI do in BI' is: AI is excellent at the mechanical and the first-draft, and weak at judgment and context. Well-suited tasks: drafting a DAX or SQL query from a plain-English description (you still verify it), explaining an unfamiliar function or error, and generating boilerplate like documentation or repetitive transformations, work where the answer is checkable and the cost of a wrong draft is low. items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## Proof of work beats a list of skills

Anyone can type "Power BI, SQL, DAX" on a CV. Almost nobody can show a real dashboard, explain the design decisions, and walk through the DAX or SQL behind it. The people who *can* get the interviews. This week you stop being a list of skills and become a body of evidence.

A BI portfolio has to demonstrate three things, and a hiring manager is scanning for all three. **Technical skill:** can you build a complete, well-structured report or pipeline, not a tutorial copy, but your own clean model, measures, and queries? **Analytical thinking:** can you find an insight that matters and explain *why* it matters, the "so what"? **Communication:** can you present data so a decision-maker acts on it? Notice these map exactly onto the last fourteen weeks, the modelling, the statistics, the storytelling. You already did the work; now you make it legible.

The good news is you are not starting from zero. You have a published Superstore dashboard, SQL reporting views, an A/B test analysis, a reproducible pandas notebook, and a cloud BI report. That is already more than most junior candidates show. This week's job is **curation and narration**: pick the strongest pieces, and for each one write the story, the question it answered, the decisions you made, and what you would do next.

The reframe for the week: a portfolio is not a folder of files, it is a set of *arguments* that you can do the job. Every artefact needs a sentence answering "why should a hiring manager care?" A dashboard with no context is wallpaper; a dashboard with "this revealed that Central's margin was bleeding on discounts, and here's the fix I'd recommend" is an interview.

Today, orient: list every artefact you have built across the program, and beside each write one sentence, the business question it answers. The pieces with the sharpest sentences are your portfolio headliners; the ones where you struggle to write the sentence probably do not belong.

items.title: BI portfolio requirements
items.body:
## What a strong BI portfolio actually contains

A portfolio is not "everything I ever built", it is a curated set of 3 to 5 pieces, each chosen to prove a different capability, each wrapped in context. Quantity signals desperation; curation signals judgment.

**The anatomy of one good piece.** For each project, a reviewer should find, in under two minutes: the **business question** ("what is dragging down Superstore's overall margin?"), a **screenshot or live link** so they see the result without installing anything, a short **"my approach"** (the data, the model, the key measures or queries), the **insight** (what you found), and the **recommendation** (what you would do about it). The artefact plus that narration is the portfolio; the artefact alone is not.

**What to include, and the range to aim for.** Show breadth across the stack: a **Power BI dashboard** (modelling + DAX + design), a **SQL project** (the reporting views and window functions), an **analysis notebook** (pandas cleaning and EDA), and ideally the **cloud/BigQuery + Looker** piece (architecture range). Different pieces prove different muscles; together they say "I can work end to end".

**The cardinal sins.** A dashboard with no context (the reviewer has no idea why it exists). Tutorial clones presented as your own (interviewers recognise the Superstore-from-a-YouTube-video instantly, your *own* analytical angle is what saves it). Broken links and "request access" walls, if they cannot see it in one click, it does not exist. And volume over quality: five polished pieces beat twenty half-finished ones every time.

**Make it skimmable.** Hiring managers spend seconds, not minutes, on a first pass. Lead each project with the screenshot and the one-sentence question. Put the technical depth below for the people who choose to dig, the pyramid principle from your storytelling week, applied to your own career.

Today: pick your **3 to 5 headliner pieces** and, for one of them, write the full wrapper, question, screenshot, approach, insight, recommendation. That template is what you will replicate for the rest this week.

items.title: GitHub for BI analysts
items.body:
## GitHub for analysts: yes, even for BI

"I work in Power BI, why GitHub?" Because GitHub is where technical hiring managers look to see *how you work*, not just what you produced. For a BI analyst it is both a portfolio host and a credibility signal: it says you understand version control, documentation, and reproducibility, the habits that separate a professional from someone clicking around a desktop tool.

**What goes in a BI repo.** The `.pbix` file is binary and large, so the repo is really about everything *around* it: a strong **README** (the project's question, approach, screenshots, and findings, this is the page that gets read), your **SQL files** (the reporting views and queries, which *are* diffable and reviewable), your **pandas notebooks** (rendered, GitHub displays them), and **data documentation** (the schema, the data dictionary, the measure definitions). A screenshot or GIF of the dashboard embedded in the README does the job the binary file cannot.

**The README is the deliverable.** Most reviewers will read your README and never open anything else. Structure it like a portfolio entry: the business question up top, a screenshot, "how it's built", key findings, and how to reproduce. A repo with a great README and no code review beats a repo with great code and a blank README, because the README is what gets seen.

**Habits that signal professionalism.** Meaningful **commit messages** (you have been writing them all program). A clean repo structure (`/sql`, `/notebooks`, `/docs`, `/screenshots`). A pinned, polished **profile README** on your GitHub homepage that links your best pieces. None of this is advanced, and precisely because most BI candidates skip it, doing it sets you apart.

Today: take one project and give it a real GitHub home, a structured repo with an embedded dashboard screenshot, your SQL, and a README written as a portfolio entry. Then pin it on your profile. That repo is now a link you can drop into any application.

items.title: LinkedIn optimisation for BI roles
items.body:
## LinkedIn: the front door recruiters walk through

For BI roles, most first contact happens on LinkedIn, recruiters search it, screen it, and decide whether to reach out before you ever apply. A profile that is invisible to that search costs you opportunities you never even see. Optimising it is not vanity; it is being findable for the jobs you want.

**Get found: keywords where the search looks.** Recruiters search on titles and skills, so the words "Power BI", "SQL", "DAX", "data analyst", "business intelligence" must appear in your **headline**, **about**, and **experience**, not buried in a skills list. Your headline is prime real estate: "Business Intelligence Analyst | Power BI, SQL, DAX | turning data into decisions" beats "Aspiring data professional" because it matches what a recruiter actually types.

**Convert once found: the About section.** Two or three short paragraphs in plain English, who you are, what you build, and a concrete proof point ("built an end-to-end Power BI sales dashboard that surfaced a margin leak in the Central region"). Specificity sells; "passionate about data" is noise everyone writes.

**Show the work.** Use the **Featured** section to pin links to your portfolio pieces, the GitHub repo, the live Looker report, a dashboard screenshot. A recruiter who can click straight to proof is a recruiter who shortlists you.

**Signal activity and credibility.** A professional photo, a banner, and the occasional post about something you built ("here's what I learned modelling a star schema") keep you visible in feeds and show you are engaged, not dormant. Recommendations and listed skills add social proof.

The mindset: your profile is a **landing page for one product, you**, optimised for one conversion, "this person can do BI, let's talk". Every section should serve that.

Today: rewrite your **headline** and **About** with real keywords and one concrete proof point, and pin your two best artefacts to Featured. Then search LinkedIn for "BI analyst" yourself, see whose profiles surface, and borrow what works.

items.title: BI interview question types
items.body:
## What BI interviews actually test, and how to prepare

BI interviews are predictable once you know the four buckets they draw from. Prepare for each deliberately and you walk in calm instead of hoping.

**Technical SQL.** The most common live test. Expect to write joins, GROUP BY with aggregation, and especially **window functions** (running totals, rank, "top N per group") and CTEs, exactly your W7 material. Practice writing these out loud on a whiteboard or in a shared editor, talking through your logic, because they assess *how you think*, not just the final query. Sites like StrataScratch and LeetCode's database section mirror the format.

**DAX / tool-specific.** "Write a measure for year-over-year growth", "what's the difference between a calculated column and a measure?", "explain filter context." These reward the modelling fundamentals you built, and the honest "here's how I'd reason about filter context" answer beats a memorised formula.

**Case study / analytical thinking.** "Our conversion dropped 15% last month, how would you investigate?" There is no single right answer; they want a **structured approach**, clarify the metric, segment to localise the drop, form hypotheses, decide what data would confirm each. This is where your storytelling and statistics weeks pay off, you reason like an analyst, not a chart-maker.

**Behavioural / stakeholder.** "Tell me about a time your analysis changed a decision", "how do you handle a stakeholder who wants a chart that misleads?" Answer with the **STAR** structure (Situation, Task, Action, Result) and use your *real* project stories, the Central-margin insight, the dashboard redesign. Specific beats generic every time.

**The meta-skill: think out loud.** Across all four, interviewers are watching your reasoning. A wrong answer reached through clear, structured thinking often scores better than a right answer with no explanation. Narrate your approach.

Today: write out **STAR answers for three behavioural questions** using your actual program projects, and do **two SQL window-function problems** out loud, talking through each step. You are rehearsing the format, not just the content.

items.title: Salary negotiation and career progression in BI
items.body:
## Knowing your worth: salary and the path beyond junior

Two career skills get neglected and cost real money over time: negotiating the offer, and understanding where the role leads. Both are worth a day.

**Negotiation, the basics that matter.** First, **know the range** before you talk numbers, use Levels.fyi, Glassdoor, and local salary surveys for "BI analyst" in your market, because an offer you cannot benchmark is one you cannot judge. Second, **let them name a number first** where you can; "what's the budgeted range for this role?" is a fair, normal question. Third, when an offer comes, **it is almost always negotiable**, a polite, specific counter ("based on my Power BI and SQL portfolio and the market range, could we move base to X?") is expected, not offensive, and the worst case is "no". Fourth, **evaluate the whole package**, base, bonus, learning budget, remote flexibility, the title (which shapes your *next* job), not just the headline number.

**The progression ladder.** BI is a career with a clear path, and knowing it helps you negotiate the *direction* as well as the pay. The common arc: **BI Analyst** (build reports, answer questions) → **Senior BI Analyst** (own a domain, mentor, design metrics) → and then a fork: toward **Analytics Engineer / BI Developer** (deeper technical, dbt, data modelling, pipelines) or toward **Analytics Manager / BI Lead** (strategy, stakeholders, leading a team). Adjacent jumps into **data engineering** or **product analytics** are common too.

**Steer on purpose.** Early roles shape the fork you take, so weigh "what will I learn and who will I work with?" alongside salary. A slightly lower-paying role with a strong mentor and modern stack can outperform a higher-paying dead-end within two years. You are negotiating a trajectory, not a single number.

Today: **benchmark the salary range** for BI analyst roles in your target market and write it down, then draft the two or three sentences you would actually say to counter an offer. Rehearsing the words now means you will not freeze when it counts.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Ship it

Package the week into a **complete, public job-search kit**, the artefact that turns fifteen weeks of building into interviews.

Produce:
- **A portfolio home** (site or GitHub profile) linking 3 to 5 curated pieces, each wrapped with its business question, a screenshot/live link, your approach, the insight, and a recommendation.
- **At least one project in a polished GitHub repo** with a README written as a portfolio entry (question, screenshot, how it's built, findings, reproduce steps) and a clean structure.
- **An optimised LinkedIn profile**: keyword-rich headline and About, two artefacts pinned to Featured, a real proof point in the summary.
- **An interview-prep doc**: STAR answers for 3 behavioural questions using your real projects, plus notes on the four BI-interview buckets and your benchmarked salary range.

Commit the kit:

```
git add portfolio/ && git commit -m "BI: portfolio + job-search kit (curated projects, GitHub README, LinkedIn, interview prep)"
git push
```

This is the week that converts skill into offers. Most candidates with similar skills never package them, so a clean portfolio, a findable LinkedIn, and rehearsed interview answers put you ahead of people who can do the same work but cannot prove it. items.body: Walking an interviewer through your most complex DAX measure is really a test of whether you understand your own work or just got it to run. items.title: Set up your tooling
items.body:
## What it is
The capstone is a complete, end-to-end BI project on a dataset *you* choose, not Superstore. This setup day is about choosing your **tool stack** deliberately: where the data will live (a file, BigQuery, a database), what you will model and visualise in (Power BI, Looker Studio), and where the code and docs will live (a GitHub repo). Pick the stack that fits *your* dataset and the story you want to tell.

## What you'll do today
- Decide your stack: source → modelling/viz tool → repo. For most, that is "CSV or BigQuery → Power BI → GitHub", but choose for your project
- Create the capstone GitHub repo with a skeleton structure (`/data`, `/sql`, `/docs`, `/screenshots`, `README.md`)
- Confirm each tool in the chosen stack opens and connects
- Commit a `day0` README stub naming your stack and a one-line project idea

## Why before anything else
A capstone stalls when the stack is half-decided and you discover on Day 4 that your tool cannot read your data. Lock the pipeline today, on an empty project, so the rest of the week is analysis and building, not tooling surprises.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## Your project, your question, from scratch

For fifteen weeks Superstore gave you a safe, pre-cleaned sandbox. The capstone takes the training wheels off: you choose a dataset you actually care about, sports, finance, health, public government data, your own business numbers, and you build a complete BI project on it end to end. This is the piece your whole portfolio will be anchored around, so choose something you can talk about with genuine interest, because that energy shows in an interview.

The single most important principle: **a good BI project starts with a question, not a dataset.** Amateurs grab data and ask "what can I show?"; professionals start with a sharp analytical question and gather data to answer it. Strong questions sound like "What drives customer churn?", "Which products are quietly dragging down overall margin?", "Where in the funnel are we losing users?" Each is specific, decision-oriented, and gives every visual in your eventual report a job: it either helps answer the question or it gets cut.

This week (W16) is **design and build the prototype**. The deliverable by Sunday is *not* a polished dashboard, it is a **working prototype** with your question at its centre: data sourced and loaded, a sensible model, and a first version of the report that begins to answer the question. Next week (W17) is polish, performance, documentation, and presentation. Resist the urge to perfect visuals now; get the spine working first.

A realistic scope warning: with one to two weeks, pick a question you can *actually* answer with data you can *actually* get. "Solve climate change" is not a capstone; "which factors correlate with higher player scores in this season's dataset?" is. Narrow and finished beats broad and abandoned, every reviewer prefers a sharp, complete small project to an ambitious half-built one.

Today, orient: write your **capstone brief**, one paragraph, in your README: the analytical question, why it matters, the dataset you will use, and what a good answer would let someone *do*. If you cannot write that paragraph crisply, the project is not scoped yet, fix that before you touch the data.

items.title: Project scoping
items.body:
## Scoping: the discipline that finishes projects

Most failed capstones do not fail in the building, they fail in the scoping. Either the question is too big to answer in the time, or it is so vague that no result ever feels like "done". Scoping is the act of carving a sharp, finishable project out of a fuzzy idea, and it is a senior skill worth practising deliberately.

**Sharpen the question.** Move from a topic to a question to a *measurable* question. "Customer behaviour" (topic) → "what drives churn?" (question) → "which customer attributes best separate churned from retained customers in the last 12 months?" (measurable). The last version tells you exactly what data you need and what a result looks like. If you cannot picture the chart that answers your question, sharpen it further.

**Define done.** Write the **deliverable** explicitly: "a Power BI report with three pages that answers the churn question, plus a one-paragraph recommendation." A project with a written definition of done can be finished; one without expands forever, because "a bit more" is always tempting.

**Right-size the scope.** Honestly estimate against your time and skills. A good capstone has **one central question and two or three supporting ones**, not ten. When in doubt, cut, a narrow project done well demonstrates more competence than a broad one left ragged. Reviewers read "finished and sharp" as professional and "sprawling and incomplete" as a warning.

**Name your assumptions and risks up front.** "I'm assuming this public dataset is reasonably complete; the risk is missing months, which I'll check on Day 3." Surfacing risks early is how you avoid discovering a fatal data gap the night before the deadline.

Today: write a **one-page project scope** in your repo, the sharpened measurable question, the explicit definition of done, the two or three supporting questions, and your top assumptions and risks. This page is the contract you hold yourself to all week.

items.title: Data source evaluation and ingestion planning
items.body:
## Sourcing data: where it comes from and whether you can trust it

A capstone is only as good as its data, and real data, unlike Superstore, arrives messy, incomplete, or hard to get. Today you evaluate sources and plan ingestion *before* committing, so you do not build a beautiful report on a broken foundation.

**Where to find data.** Public, capstone-friendly sources include government open-data portals (data.gov and national equivalents), Kaggle datasets, the World Bank and other agency APIs, sports-stats sites, and your own exported data from a tool you use. Prefer a source that is **rich enough to ask a real question of** (multiple dimensions and a decent time span) over a tiny, toy table.

**Evaluate before you commit.** Run a quick due-diligence pass: **completeness** (how many nulls, how many missing periods?), **granularity** (is it at the row level you need, or pre-aggregated past the point of usefulness?), **freshness and span** (does it cover enough time to show a trend?), **licence** (are you allowed to use and publish it?), and **trustworthiness** (who produced it, and could it be biased or wrong?). A spreadsheet of red flags now saves a dead-end on Day 5.

**Plan ingestion.** Decide *how* the data gets into your tool and write it down: a one-off CSV import, a connection to a database, an API pull into pandas, or a load into BigQuery. Note any cleaning you already know you will need, type fixes, deduplication, standardising categories, the W12 cleaning skills applied to *your* data. If the ingestion needs to repeat (a refreshable source), sketch how, the W4 scheduled-refresh thinking.

**Have a fallback.** If your first-choice dataset turns out too broken to use, know your plan B *today*, not at the deadline. Professionals de-risk the data before investing days of modelling on top of it.

Today: **acquire and profile your dataset**, load it, run `head/shape/info` (or the tool's equivalent), count nulls and duplicates, and write a short **data-source assessment** in your docs: where it came from, its quality, its licence, and your ingestion plan. If it fails the assessment, switch now.

items.title: End-to-end BI architecture
items.body:
## Architecture: the spine the whole project hangs on

Before placing a single visual, design the **end-to-end architecture**, the path from raw source to a number on screen. Every BI project has the same backbone, and naming yours keeps the build coherent instead of accidental.

**The five stages.** *Source* (where data originates) → *Ingestion* (how it lands: import, API, load) → *Transformation* (cleaning and shaping: Power Query, SQL, pandas) → *Model* (the star schema, relationships, and measures) → *Presentation* (the report and its story). You have built every stage across the program; the capstone is the first time *you* design the whole chain for a new dataset.

**Model deliberately, the lesson that decides everything downstream.** Apply your W8 modelling: separate **facts** (the events you measure, sales, matches, transactions) from **dimensions** (the context you slice by, date, product, region, customer), and connect them in a **star schema**. Build a proper **date dimension** so time intelligence works. Define your core **measures** once, cleanly, in DAX or SQL. A good model makes the report easy and every later question answerable; a bad model means you fight the tool for the rest of the project. The single most common capstone mistake is dumping one wide flat table and then struggling to compute anything, do not do that.

**Design for the question.** The architecture should be the *shortest correct path* to answering your scoped question. Do not model dimensions you will never slice by; do not build pages your question does not need. Architecture is as much about what you leave out as what you include.

**Write it down.** A simple diagram, source → ingest → transform → model → present, with the tool named at each stage, is worth more than it looks: it catches gaps (where exactly does cleaning happen?) before they become rework, and it is exactly the kind of artefact that impresses in an interview.

Today: **draw your architecture diagram** and **build the data model**, the star schema with facts, dimensions, a date table, and your core measures defined. By end of day you should be able to compute your headline metric correctly. That is the spine; tomorrow's report just renders it.

days.summary: Focus: Documentation standards for BI projects

items.title: Documentation standards for BI projects
items.body:
## Documentation: the difference between a project and a portfolio piece

Undocumented BI work is a liability: six months on, nobody, including you, remembers what a measure means or why a number was filtered. Documentation is what turns a one-off dashboard into something a team can trust, maintain, and hire you for. It is also, bluntly, what reviewers read, so it is worth doing well.

**The data dictionary.** For each table and key column, record what it *is*: name, type, meaning, source, and any transformation applied ("`revenue` = gross sales minus returns, in USD, from the orders table"). This is the first thing a new analyst, or an interviewer, looks for, because it tells them whether they can trust your numbers.

**Measure / metric definitions.** Document every important measure in plain English *and* its formula: "Profit Margin % = total profit / total sales, blank when sales = 0." This kills the classic disease of two dashboards disagreeing because "margin" was defined differently, the governance idea from your Looker week, applied at project scale.

**The decision log.** Record the *judgment calls*: "excluded 2019 because the data was incomplete", "treated null discount as zero because the source omits zero-discount orders." These decisions are invisible in the final report but explain every number, and being able to point to them is exactly what makes a stakeholder, or an interviewer, trust your work.

**The README as the front door.** The repo README ties it together: the question, the approach, screenshots, key findings, and how to reproduce. Most people read only this, so write it as the executive summary of the whole project.

The standard to hold: **someone else should be able to understand, trust, and rebuild your project from your docs alone.** That is the bar for professional BI, and meeting it on your capstone is a strong signal you can meet it on the job.

Today: write the **data dictionary, the measure definitions, and a decision log** for your capstone so far, in `/docs`. Keep them updated as you build, documenting at the end is how details get lost.

items.title: Version control with Git for BI
items.body:
## Version control for BI: track the project like an engineer

You have used Git all program; the capstone is where you make it *deliberate*, because a documented, well-committed repo is itself a portfolio signal. It tells a technical hiring manager you work like a professional, not someone emailing `dashboard_final_v3.pbix` to themselves.

**What Git does and does not handle well for BI.** Git shines on **text**: SQL files, pandas notebooks, documentation, configuration, all diffable, reviewable, and recoverable. It handles **binary** files like `.pbix` poorly, they are large and Git cannot show a meaningful diff, so treat the repo as the home for *everything around* the dashboard (SQL, docs, screenshots, the README) and store the `.pbix` itself there as a whole-file artefact (or via Git LFS / a linked location if it is large). The point is the surrounding work being version-controlled, not pretending Git can diff a binary.

**Commit with intent.** Small, meaningful commits with clear messages, "add date dimension and core margin measures", "fix null handling in returns join", give you a readable history and a safety net: when a number breaks, you can find the commit that broke it. This is the same habit you have practised; the capstone is where you show it off.

**Structure the repo so a stranger can navigate it.** A clean layout, `/data` (or a note on where data lives), `/sql`, `/notebooks`, `/docs`, `/screenshots`, and a strong `README.md`, signals care. A `.gitignore` keeps junk (large temp files, credentials) out. **Never commit secrets**, API keys, connection strings, database passwords, use environment variables or a config file that is git-ignored. A leaked credential in a public capstone repo is a real, avoidable mistake.

**Use the history as a narrative.** Your commit log tells the story of how the project was built, and a coherent log is quietly impressive in an interview. It shows process, not just output.

Today: **bring your capstone repo to a professional standard**, clean structure, a `.gitignore` that excludes secrets and junk, meaningful commits for the work so far, and a README that orients a stranger. Push it; this repo is now a live portfolio link.

- **A profiled dataset** with a data-source assessment (quality, licence, ingestion plan), loaded and cleaned with documented decisions.
- **An architecture diagram** and a **working data model**, a star schema with facts, dimensions, a date table, and core measures that compute your headline metric *correctly*.
- **A first-draft report** that begins to answer the question, rough visuals are fine; a correct spine matters more than polish.
- **Documentation**: data dictionary, measure definitions, decision log, and a README that orients a stranger.

Commit the milestone:

```
git add capstone/ && git commit -m "BI capstone v1: scope, data assessment, model, first-draft report + docs"
git push
```

You are deliberately *not* done, and that is correct. The discipline this week is building the right foundation: a sharp question, trustworthy data, a sound model, and honest docs. A prototype on solid footing finishes well next week; a pretty dashboard on a bad model never recovers.

Next week: complete and present, polish, performance, documentation, and the presentation that turns your analysis into something stakeholders act on.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## The week the work becomes communicable

Last week you built a working prototype on a solid model. This week you *finish* it, and the centre of gravity shifts from analysis to **communication**. Here is the hard truth that governs the week: a BI report nobody understands is a failed report, no matter how elegant the data model or how clever the DAX. The deliverable is not the dashboard; it is the *decision the dashboard enables*, and that only happens if you communicate it well.

You have two audiences, and they want different things. A **technical peer** (the analyst or engineer reviewing your work) cares about the data model, the measures, the data-quality decisions, can they trust and rebuild it? A **business stakeholder** (the manager who acts on it) cares about the answer to your question and what to *do* about it, they do not want to hear about your star schema. The skill this week is serving both: rigour underneath for the technical reviewer, a clear "so what / now what" on top for the decision-maker. Practise both registers, because real BI roles demand both.

This week's deliverables are three: a **finished, polished report** (visuals tightened, performance acceptable, the question clearly answered); a **stakeholder presentation** (the deck or recorded walkthrough that lands the insight and the recommendation); and a **written retrospective** (what worked, what you would do differently, what you want to learn next). That last one matters more than it looks, an analyst who can honestly critique their own work is one who will keep improving, and interviewers probe for exactly that self-awareness.

The mindset for the week: you are not "making it pretty", you are **removing every obstacle between your insight and the viewer's understanding**. Every polish decision, every slide, every word of documentation serves that one goal.

Today, orient: write the **single sentence** that is your capstone's headline finding and recommendation, "X is happening, driven by Y, so we should do Z." If you cannot state it in one sentence, the analysis is not finished, fix that first, because everything you build this week exists to deliver that sentence.

items.title: Dashboard polish
items.body:
## Polish: making the dashboard effortless to read

Polish is not decoration, it is the systematic removal of friction between your insight and the viewer's understanding. A polished dashboard feels *easy*; the work is in making it so. Apply your W11 design lessons to your own capstone, hard, because this is the version people will judge.

**Visual hierarchy first.** The most important number, your headline finding, should be the first thing the eye lands on: top-left, large, with a clear label. Supporting detail goes below and around it. If a stranger cannot find your key insight in five seconds, the hierarchy has failed, rebuild it before touching anything else.

**Ruthless consistency.** One accent colour for what matters, muted greys for context; consistent number formatting (decimals, currency, thousands separators) everywhere; aligned-to-a-grid layout with no ragged edges; right-aligned numbers, left-aligned text. Inconsistency reads as carelessness and quietly erodes trust in the numbers themselves.

**Cut the clutter.** Every element that does not help answer the question is *subtracting* from the ones that do. Remove decorative chart junk, redundant visuals, unnecessary gridlines and legends, and any "nice to have" that dilutes the message. The test for each visual: which question does this answer? If you cannot say, delete it.

**Label for self-sufficiency.** Clear titles that state the *takeaway* ("Central margin fell on heavy discounting") not just the dimension ("Margin by Region"); axis labels and units; a note on the data source and the as-of date. A good dashboard explains itself with no narrator present, because often there will not be one.

**Then test it on a human.** Show it to someone unfamiliar and ask, "what is this telling you, and what would you do?" Their confusion is your to-do list. This single step catches more problems than another hour of solo tweaking.

Today: do a **full polish pass** on your capstone, hierarchy, consistency, decluttering, self-explanatory labels, then test it on one person and fix whatever confused them.

items.title: Performance optimisation
items.body:
## Performance: a dashboard people will actually wait for

A slow dashboard is an unused dashboard. If a report takes ten seconds to load or lags on every click, stakeholders abandon it, and your analysis dies unseen. Performance is part of the deliverable, not an afterthought, and the capstone is where you prove you can tune it.

**Fix the model first, it is where most slowness lives.** A clean **star schema** is faster than a wide flat table because the engine filters small dimension tables instead of scanning millions of fact rows, the W8 lesson, now paying off in milliseconds. **Drop columns you never use**; every unused column bloats the model and the refresh. Set correct **data types** (a number stored as text is both slow and wrong). Where possible, **pre-aggregate**, summarise in SQL or a scheduled query so the report reads a small result rather than re-crunching raw rows on every interaction (the W13 cloud-cost discipline, applied to speed).

**Write measures that do not fight the engine.** Inefficient DAX, especially heavy use of row-by-row iterators or repeated `CALCULATE` over large tables, can make a single visual crawl. Prefer simple aggregations; reach for iterators only when truly needed. If one visual is slow, it is usually one measure, find it and simplify it.

**Trim the report surface.** Too many visuals on one page means too many simultaneous queries on every load; consolidate. Limit slicer cardinality (a slicer with 10,000 items is slow); use a date range instead of listing every day. Fewer, sharper visuals are both faster *and* better communication, performance and clarity pulling the same direction.

**Measure, do not guess.** Use the tool's diagnostics, Power BI's **Performance Analyzer** shows exactly which visual and which query are slow, so you tune the real bottleneck instead of optimising at random.

Today: **run a performance pass** on your capstone, check load and interaction speed, use Performance Analyzer (or your tool's equivalent) to find the slowest visual, and fix the top one or two bottlenecks (a measure, an unused column, a missing pre-aggregation). Note the before/after; that improvement is a real engineering result worth mentioning in an interview.

items.title: Writing BI project documentation
items.body:
## Final documentation: the project that explains itself

This is the documentation that ships, the version a stranger, a teammate, or an interviewer reads to understand and trust your work without you in the room. You drafted docs as you built (W16); today you finish them to a professional standard, because for most reviewers the docs *are* the project.

**The README as executive summary.** The repo README is the front door and the most-read artefact you will produce. Structure it as the whole project in miniature: the **question** and why it matters; a **screenshot or GIF** of the dashboard up top (so the result is visible in one second); a short **approach** (data, model, key measures); the **key findings**; the **recommendation**; and **how to reproduce** (data source, tools, steps). Someone should grasp the entire project from the README alone.

**The supporting docs, completed.** Finalise the **data dictionary** (every table and key column: meaning, type, source, transformation), the **measure definitions** (plain English plus formula for each), and the **decision log** (the judgment calls and why, the exclusions, the null-handling, the assumptions). These are what let a technical reviewer *trust* your numbers, and trust is what gets you hired.

**Write for the reader who is not you.** The test is concrete: hand your repo to someone who has never seen it and ask them to explain what the project does and whether they believe the headline number. Where they hesitate, your docs have a gap. Plain language beats jargon; a diagram beats a paragraph; a worked example beats an abstract description.

**This is a differentiator, not a chore.** Most BI candidates ship an undocumented dashboard. A capstone with a crisp README, a real data dictionary, and an honest decision log signals that you work to a professional standard, which is exactly the signal that converts a portfolio into an offer.

Today: **finish all project documentation** to the "a stranger could understand and rebuild this" bar, README, data dictionary, measure definitions, decision log, and commit it. Then have one person read only the docs and tell you what the project does; fix whatever they got wrong.

items.title: Presenting BI work to stakeholders
items.body:
## Presenting: the moment the analysis pays off

The presentation is the highest-leverage skill in BI and the one most analysts neglect. The same finding, presented well versus badly, is the difference between a decision made and a meeting forgotten. Today you learn to deliver, because your capstone, and your career, are judged on whether people *act* on your work.

**Lead with the answer (the pyramid principle).** Open with your conclusion and recommendation, not a tour of your methodology. "Margin is being eroded in the Central region by over-discounting; I recommend capping discounts on two sub-categories, which the data suggests recovers about four points." *Then* show the evidence for those who want it. Stakeholders are busy; give them the "so what" in the first thirty seconds, and earn their attention for the detail.

**Structure as a story (Situation, Insight, Action).** *Situation*: the shared context everyone agrees on. *Insight*: the surprising or uncomfortable finding your analysis uncovered, the moment they lean in. *Action*: the concrete recommendation, what to do now. This is your W11 storytelling frame, applied live; it works because it ends where decisions are made.

**Tailor to the audience in the room.** For a **business stakeholder**, minimise jargon, lead with impact and the recommendation, and be ready for "what should we do?" For a **technical peer**, be ready to defend the model, the measures, and the data-quality calls, "why did you exclude 2019?", "how is margin defined?". Knowing which audience you have, and switching register, is the senior move.

**Anticipate the hard questions.** "How confident are you?", "what's the data quality?", "what would change your recommendation?" Prepare honest answers, including the limitations. Acknowledging what your analysis *cannot* say builds far more trust than overclaiming, and overclaiming is how analysts lose credibility the first time a number proves shaky.

**Rehearse out loud.** Record yourself (this is what Loom is for) presenting the dashboard in three to five minutes. Watch it back, you will catch the rambling, the buried lede, the slide that does not land, and tighten them. A rehearsed walkthrough is also a portfolio artefact you can send with applications.

Today: **build and deliver your capstone presentation**, a short deck or a recorded Loom walkthrough that leads with the recommendation, tells the Situation-Insight-Action story, and is tailored to a decision-maker. Rehearse it at least once on camera and refine.

items.title: Continuous improvement
items.body:
## The retrospective: the habit that compounds for a career

The final deliverable is not a chart, it is **reflection**. An analyst who can honestly critique their own work is one who keeps getting better; one who cannot plateaus. The retrospective is where you turn a finished capstone into durable learning, and it is exactly the self-awareness interviewers probe with "what would you do differently?"

**Write an honest project retrospective.** Three questions, answered candidly in your repo: **What worked?** (the model that made analysis easy, the question that was well-scoped). **What would you do differently?** (the dataset you should have vetted harder, the page you over-built, the time you lost to a tooling surprise). **What did you learn?** (the technique that clicked, the mistake you will not repeat). Specific and honest beats flattering and vague, "I under-scoped the data check and lost a day" is worth more than "it went well", and it reads as maturity, not weakness.

**Then plan what's next, deliberately.** You have finished a 17-week program; momentum is precious and easy to lose. Name the next skills to develop, deeper SQL and data modelling, dbt and analytics engineering, a specific domain (finance, product, marketing analytics), or stronger statistics, and pick the *one* you will start next, with a concrete first step. A vague "keep learning" fades; "next, I'll learn dbt by rebuilding my capstone's transforms in it" gets done.

**Make reflection a standing habit, not a one-off.** The best analysts run a mini-retro after every real project: what did I learn, what would I change? Over a career that compounding is the difference between someone with ten years of experience and someone with one year repeated ten times. Your capstone retrospective is the first rep of a habit worth keeping for good.

Today: **write your capstone retrospective** (what worked, what you'd change, what you learned) and a short **learning roadmap** naming the next skill and your first concrete step toward it. Commit both; they close the program and open whatever comes next.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Ship it

This is the final ship of the program, package the **complete capstone** into the centrepiece of your portfolio.

Your finished capstone repo should contain:
- **A polished, performant report** that clearly answers your scoped question, visual hierarchy tuned, consistent formatting, decluttered, self-explanatory labels, and acceptable load/interaction speed.
- **A stakeholder presentation**: a short deck and/or a recorded Loom walkthrough that leads with the recommendation and tells the Situation-Insight-Action story.
- **Complete documentation**: a README that works as an executive summary (question, screenshot, approach, findings, recommendation, reproduce steps), plus the data dictionary, measure definitions, and decision log.
- **A retrospective and a learning roadmap**: an honest what-worked / what-you'd-change / what-you-learned, and the next skill with a concrete first step.

Commit the finale:

```
git add capstone/ && git commit -m "BI capstone: complete - polished report, presentation, full docs, retrospective"
git push
```

Then make this the headline of your portfolio and pin it on GitHub and LinkedIn. This single project demonstrates everything the program taught, a sharp question, a sound model, trustworthy data, a clear story, and honest reflection, on a dataset *you* chose. It is the strongest possible answer to "show me something you built."

That is the program. You can model data, write DAX and SQL, run an experiment, build on a cloud warehouse, use AI responsibly, and, hardest of all, turn correct numbers into decisions people act on. You have the artefacts to prove it. Go get the interview, and keep the retro habit, it is what turns a first BI job into a BI career.

cards.prompt: The fastest way to learn a new tool is to read the docs end-to-end before writing any code.
cards.whenRight: Right - building a tiny example first beats reading every page.
cards.whenWrong: Docs are a reference, not a tutorial. Code first, read second.

cards.prompt: Committing small checkpoints helps you debug regressions and review your own progress.
cards.whenRight: Exactly - tiny commits are a superpower.
cards.whenWrong: They really do help; `git revert` is one command away.

cards.prompt: Copy-pasting from Stack Overflow without understanding is a sustainable long-term strategy.
cards.whenRight: Correct - understanding the why is what makes you employable.
cards.whenWrong: Short-term it works; long-term it stalls you.

items.title: Finish and ship the week's project
items.body:
[PRODUCE] Capstone Delivery: Deliver your complete BI solution including: (1) Published dashboard (Tableau Public or Power BI Service), (2) GitHub repository with full documentation, (3) 5-minute demo video, (4) Written business report. Share all links in your LinkedIn profile and GitHub README.

Ship checklist:
 - It runs from a clean clone / fresh open, no "works on my machine" steps missing.
 - Commit it to your repo with a short README saying what it does and how to run it.
 - Tag or note this as your Week 17 deliverable so you can look back on it.

PASS:
[x] You completed the task described above
[x] You can explain in one sentence what you produced
[x] Your work is committed to your repo

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: The most important insight from your capstone is the one sentence a stakeholder would remember a week later, and being able to state it, with honest confidence, is the whole point of the project. So give it to me sharply: not 'sales vary by region' but 'the West region's margin is being silently eroded by discounting, and it is the single biggest drag on company profit'. Then do the thing that separates an analyst from a chart-maker: tell me how confident you are and why. What is the strength of the evidence, and just as importantly, what would invalidate it, a data-quality issue, a confounding variable, too small a sample, a correlation you have not proven causal? State your single most important insight, your confidence level, and the specific finding or error that would overturn it.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:

```bash
git add . && git commit -m 'Capstone Project, Week 2: Complete and Present'
git tag v17.0 && git push --tags
```
